title: Grade 8 daily reading
overview: An independent nightly reading year pairs authentic narrative and poetry with literary natural history. Short poems invite repeated oral reading; prose selections pause at meaningful episodes rather than fixed lengths. The early sequence develops attentive quotation and distinctions between observation and inference; later selections ask for more independent interpretation of motives, perspective, and evidence. The 20–25 minute budgets include discussion and are editorial estimates, not measured completion times. Historical wording and assumptions are identified outside the source text. Excerpts provide sustained local reading and return visits to authors, rather than claiming that whole novels are supplied.

progression.focus: Close attention to narrative voice, figurative language, and observation.
progression.rationale: The first band alternates a familiar narrative situation, descriptive essays, and short poems. Readers distinguish what is reported from what a narrator or speaker infers, using a clearly named textual detail before extending an interpretation.

progression.focus: Motives, incomplete knowledge, and the shape of an episode.
progression.rationale: Adventure episodes ask readers to track action, working knowledge, and motives across several paragraphs. Dickens’s remembered scenes and Austin’s changing viewpoints continue the distinction between an experience and its interpretation; late-band poems test social satire and conflicting impulses.

Scott’s historical fiction introduces unfamiliar institutions, narrative mediation and social expectations. London’s middle chapters, including the fight with Spitz and Dave’s death, and Doyle’s expedition supply competing explanations of action, while Wordsworth’s poems invite comparisons between a remembered experience and its later significance.

progression.focus: Memory, perspective, and patterns across a larger movement.
progression.rationale: Dickens’s Stave Three ending and complete Stave Four run on consecutive nights, from Ignorance and Want through old Joe’s shop, the Cratchits’ mourning and the neglected grave, before Stave Five. Mountain and forest essays connect setting and perspective with judgments about value, and short poems require selective rereading before Wells introduces a sustained uncertainty about evidence.

progression.focus: Limits of evidence and the consequences of framing.
progression.rationale: Speculative and adventure fiction invite scrutiny of hypotheses, analogy and narrator reliability. Doyle’s chapters on the plateau, from the night pursuit through Lord John’s account, the rescue at the cliff and the battle, ask readers to separate events from the narrator’s judgments. Natural-history essays and historical fiction add unfamiliar assumptions and syntax.

Late selections combine extended syntax, ambiguous judgments and unfamiliar forms. London’s final chapter is read whole across consecutive nights. Seven consecutive nights sustain the complete Rime of the Ancient Mariner. Wells’s Underworld and forest-fire chapters lead into his closing episodes, and Kubla Khan tests how an imaginative account can retain significance when certainty or completeness is unavailable.

days.title: A Christmas Carol — Stave One: a cold introduction
days.challenge: Separate the narrator’s playful interruptions from the facts establishing Scrooge’s isolation.
days.focus: How a comic voice and an extended coldness metaphor establish character.
days.context: The novella opens years after the death of Scrooge’s business partner, Jacob Marley.

excerpt.locator: PG 19337, dated 1905 edition; Stave One: a cold introduction; narrative paragraphs 1–9; begins "Marley was dead, to begin with. There is no doubt whatever about that. The register of his burial was signed b"; ends "hs of life, warning all human sympathy to keep its distance, was what the knowing ones call \"nuts\" to Scrooge.".

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator insist on Marley’s death before describing Scrooge?
facilitatorNotes: His certainty establishes the ordinary fact against which a later supernatural event will matter; the conversational insistence also establishes the narrator’s voice.
evidence: Marley was dead

questions.prompt: What does the comparison with an oyster suggest beyond being unfriendly?
facilitatorNotes: The closed shell suggests guarded isolation. A reader may also hear the possibility of something hidden inside, but should mark that as a possibility, not a fact established here.
evidence: solitary as an oyster

questions.prompt: How does the weather comparison turn generosity into a joke at Scrooge’s expense?
facilitatorNotes: Rain and snow at least come down generously; Scrooge never does. Physical coldness becomes a judgment about his dealings with people.
evidence: Scrooge never did.

days.title: The Land of Little Rain — a country of three seasons
days.challenge: Keep geographic description, reported measurements, and figurative claims distinct.
days.focus: How detailed observation challenges the idea that a desert is empty.
days.context: Mary Austin describes the dry country east of California’s Sierra Nevada in this 1903 essay.
days.contentNote: The passage mentions fatal desert journeys and human remains. Historical names for Indigenous peoples are retained. These are early twentieth-century observations, not current travel or survival instructions.

excerpt.locator: The Land of Little Rain — a country of three seasons; begins “East away from the Sierras, south from Panamint and Amargosa, east and south many an ”; ends “defined areas of growth, the best index the voiceless land can give the traveler of his whereabouts.”.

questions.prompt: What limitation does Austin find in the word “Desert”?
facilitatorNotes: She argues that inability to support human settlement is not absence of life; naming reflects a human-centered assumption.
evidence: Void of life it never is

questions.prompt: What does the comparison of two Amaranthus plants contribute that the phrase “cheerful adaptations” cannot establish alone?
facilitatorNotes: The reported ten-foot and four-inch plants provide a concrete example of growth varying with rainfall; the cheerful wording is interpretation.
evidence: four inches

questions.prompt: Why can plant distribution act like an index for a traveler?
facilitatorNotes: Different species correspond to slope, soil, exposure, and water. The plants make otherwise hidden local conditions readable.
evidence: the best index the voiceless land can give

questions.prompt: How do flowers function as a calendar in the opening?
facilitatorNotes: Their blooming gives the observer a locally experienced signal for expected bird arrivals, rather than a fixed date applicable everywhere.
evidence: The dandelion tells me

questions.prompt: What does the winter-wren passage establish, and what does it leave open?
facilitatorNotes: He has seen wrens far apart in place and time; he asks, rather than proves, how such a small bird completes the journey.
evidence: Does he travel by easy stages

questions.prompt: How does the bluebird’s progression from a voice to a visible nest-seeker shape the account?
facilitatorNotes: The gradual discovery lets readers experience the return through sound, uncertainty, then increasingly familiar behavior.

days.title: The Temporary the All
days.challenge: Reread inverted syntax and distinguish anticipated improvements from the life actually lived.
days.focus: Repetition of postponement and the retrospective force of a title.
days.context: Hardy’s speaker looks back on relationships, housing, and ambitions once treated as provisional.

questions.prompt: What do the imagined friend, woman, home, and life-work have in common?
facilitatorNotes: Each supposedly better future makes the present seem temporary; the domains accumulate into an entire postponed life.
evidence: Life is roomy yet

questions.prompt: Where does the speaker’s repeated self-assurance break?
facilitatorNotes: “But lo, me!” interrupts the self-quotation and leads into the recognition that the substitutes were never surpassed.
evidence: But lo, me!

questions.prompt: Does the ending blame only external fate?
facilitatorNotes: No. It names both Fate and the speaker’s own hand, leaving responsibility shared or unresolved rather than assigning a single cause.
evidence: Fate or my hand’s achieving

days.focus: Reversing the customary opposition of welcome light and frightening darkness.
days.context: Johnson imagines Night as a maternal presence that precedes the stars.

questions.prompt: What does the word “So” connect at the beginning of the second stanza?

questions.prompt: How do mother, haven, and bosom shape the ending’s emotional meaning?
facilitatorNotes: They make darkness protective and restful rather than threatening; readers can explain the metaphor without being required to share the speaker’s belief.

days.context: Burroughs considers robins and phoebes arriving among farms and sugar maples.

days.focus: Self-correction, attraction, and the limits of a purely tragic desert story.
days.context: Near the end of the opening essay, Austin considers treasure stories and her own attraction to the desert.

questions.prompt: What possibility does “to satisfy expectation” raise about writing descriptions of the desert?

questions.prompt: How do the flowers, mossy stones, and murmuring water delay the expected business of collecting nuts?
facilitatorNotes: They draw the child into lingering, receptive pleasure before he acts possessively. The long pause gives readers a felt sense of what his later action destroys.
evidence: with the flowers I played

questions.prompt: Why is the sight of the sky described as an intrusion after the branches are torn down?
facilitatorNotes: The opening now marks damage to a sheltered place. Something often associated with freedom becomes evidence of loss because the boy has changed the scene.
evidence: the intruding sky

questions.prompt: How does “unless I now / Confound my present feelings with the past” complicate the final lesson?
facilitatorNotes: The adult admits that remorse may belong partly to later reflection rather than the original moment. The lesson can remain meaningful without the memory being treated as an exact record of a childhood conversion.
evidence: Confound my present feelings with the past

days.title: Ivanhoe: Two Collars in the Forest
days.challenge: Connect detailed clothing descriptions with implied social constraints.
days.focus: The contrast between outward difference and shared bondage.
days.context: Gurth the swineherd and Wamba the jester appear in a forest clearing.
days.contentNote: This historical novel imagines twelfth-century England through nineteenth-century assumptions. Its national, religious, racial, and class generalizations are perspectives to examine, not reliable descriptions of whole peoples. Historical insults and threats appear in the original text.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, Chapter I, paragraphs 7–10 of the Wikisource transcription; opens “The sun was setting upon one of the rich grassy glades of that forest,”; closes “ the modern reader, for whose benefit we beg to offer the following translation.”.

questions.prompt: What does the fallen stone do to the brook, and how does that change the description’s sound?
facilitatorNotes: An obstruction gives an otherwise silent stream a voice. This small detail creates a living landscape rather than a static list of objects.
evidence: a feeble voice of murmur

questions.prompt: Why do the two collars matter more than the different colors and materials of the clothing?
facilitatorNotes: Both men are labeled as Cedric’s property. Wamba’s silver collar and bright clothes change appearance without removing bondage.
evidence: the thrall of Cedric of Rotherwood

questions.prompt: How does the narrator keep Gurth’s dejection from meaning simple passivity?
facilitatorNotes: The occasional fire in his eye suggests suppressed resistance beneath apparent apathy. Ask how that differs from the jester’s restless self-satisfaction.
evidence: a disposition to resistance

days.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: Ice, risk and four moccasins
days.challenge: Connect a sequence of rescues with the quieter evidence of care at its end.
days.focus: Heroism measured against environmental limits.
days.context: The team must cross the dangerous Thirty Mile River while carrying government dispatches.
days.contentNote: Near-drowning, cold injury and physical suffering, without a fatality in this passage.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 3; begins "The Thirty Mile River was wide open. Its wild water defied the"; ends "grew hard to the trail, and the worn-out foot-gear was thrown away.".

questions.prompt: Why is a quarter-mile day not evidence of idleness here?
facilitatorNotes: The cliff rescue consumes extraordinary effort; distance alone misrepresents the work needed to survive.
evidence: a quarter of a mile to the day's credit

questions.prompt: How does Perrault’s pole change the meaning of his willingness to risk the ice?
facilitatorNotes: His courage includes a practical precaution that repeatedly saves him. Discuss whether the continuing risks also expose pressure from his assignment.
evidence: the long pole he carried

questions.prompt: What does the moccasin episode add that the large rescues do not?
facilitatorNotes: Care becomes patient, individual and slightly comic: François gives his own footwear, and Buck learns to ask for protection.
evidence: his four feet waving appealingly in the air

days.title: The Lost World — excerpt: The forest as a cathedral
days.challenge: Sustain attention through a long descriptive paragraph and trace vertical space.
days.focus: Religious architecture and sensory detail in a traveller’s account.
days.context: Challenger, Summerlee, Lord John Roxton and Malone have begun their canoe journey with local guides. Malone describes entering the forest before reaching the plateau.
days.contentNote: The narrator makes broad period claims about nature and the continent. Read them as a fictional traveller’s impressions rather than current scientific reference.

excerpt.locator: Hodder and Stoughton 1912 scan-backed Wikisource text, Chapter 8, transcribed paragraphs 5–6; begins "The very next day we did actually make our start upon this remarkable expedition. We found that all our posses"; ends "tled clumsily amid the shadows. It was the only sign of earth life which I saw in this great Amazonian forest.".

questions.prompt: Why are the two professors placed in different canoes?
facilitatorNotes: The practical arrangement manages their antagonism. It links the description of Challenger’s shifting weather-like moods to the expedition’s organisation.
evidence: putting one Professor into each canoe

questions.prompt: How does the cathedral comparison change the emotional effect of the trees?
facilitatorNotes: Columns, Gothic curves, a roof and vaulted aisles turn immense vegetation into a solemn interior. Even Challenger’s whisper shows that the setting alters human behaviour.
evidence: Gothic upward curves

questions.prompt: How does the paragraph distinguish life at ground level from life above?
facilitatorNotes: Plants struggle toward light and animals move high overhead, while the travellers stumble in shade. The changing viewpoint makes the humans seem small and poorly placed to observe.
evidence: looked down in wonder at our tiny, dark, stumbling figures

days.title: A Poet’s Epitaph
days.challenge: Read the addresses aloud with distinct tones, then reconsider whom the poem excludes and finally welcomes.
days.focus: A poet’s values expressed through a procession of unsuitable and suitable visitors.
days.context: An epitaph is writing associated with a grave. Here the speaker imagines people approaching a poet’s resting place. “Statist” means a statesman in this historical usage.
days.contentNote: The poem uses satirical occupational caricatures and a disturbing image of a mother’s grave; these are rhetorical judgments to examine.

excerpt.locator: A Poet’s Epitaph, complete individual poem in volume2; HTML poem-text column beginning “Art thou a Statist in the van” and ending “Or build thy house upon this grave.”; variant, annotation and line-number columns excluded.

questions.prompt: Why must the soldier put down a sword and take a peasant’s staff before approaching?
facilitatorNotes: The exchange asks him to suspend pride and violence in favor of humility. Unlike some visitors, he is welcomed conditionally rather than simply driven away.
evidence: lay thy sword aside

questions.prompt: What connects the Moralist’s closed world to the command to shut the door and press down the latch?
facilitatorNotes: The physical enclosure repeats an inward self-sufficiency that excludes sensation and feeling. The poem criticizes reasoning when it becomes insulated from life, rather than demonstrating that all thought is bad.
evidence: Himself his world, and his own God

questions.prompt: Why can the last visitor be called weak and idle yet be allowed to build a house on the grave?
facilitatorNotes: His receptive attention and kinship with the poet matter more than public achievement. The extravagant final welcome reverses the earlier guarded distance.
evidence: The harvest of a quiet eye

days.title: Ivanhoe: When Swine Become Pork
days.challenge: Follow a joke that develops into political criticism and personal danger.
days.focus: Wordplay as a way of exposing unequal work and reward.
days.context: Gurth tries to gather his pigs while Wamba turns the task into a conversation about power.
days.contentNote: This historical novel imagines twelfth-century England through nineteenth-century assumptions. Its national, religious, racial, and class generalizations are perspectives to examine, not reliable descriptions of whole peoples. Historical insults and threats appear in the original text.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, Chapter I, paragraphs 11–28 of the Wikisource transcription; opens “"The curse of St Withold upon these infernal porkers," said the swine-”; closes “re him, with the assistance of Fangs, the whole herd of his inharmonious charge.”.

questions.prompt: What is Wamba’s real point when he says a pig becomes Norman?
facilitatorNotes: The animal’s Saxon name belongs to its care by laborers; its French name belongs to consumption by nobles. He turns a linguistic contrast into a criticism of who works and who benefits.
evidence: she goes by her Saxon name

questions.prompt: How does Wamba’s pretend consultation with his legs establish his style of resistance?
facilitatorNotes: He treats his own comfort as royal policy and uses mock dignity to refuse work. His wit makes refusal entertaining while preserving his self-interest.
evidence: I have consulted my legs

questions.prompt: What changes when Wamba imagines reporting Gurth’s words to a Norman lord?
facilitatorNotes: A playful exchange reveals the real danger of political speech. Wamba finally denies betrayal, leaving the contrast between foolishness and practical wisdom unsettled.
evidence: the trick of a wise man

days.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: The fight with Spitz
days.challenge: Trace how the narrator links a rabbit chase, a theory of “ecstasy,” and the decisive fight.
days.focus: Instinct and imagination in London’s account of mastery.
days.context: Buck and the lead dog Spitz have been rivals since the beach at Dyea. On the trail to Dawson Buck has openly undermined Spitz’s leadership, and discipline in the team has broken down.
days.contentNote: Dogs chase and kill a rabbit, and Buck and Spitz fight to the death while a circle of huskies waits to close in on the loser. The violence is vivid.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 3; begins "At the mouth of the Tahkeena, one night after supper, Dub turned up a "; ends "champion, the dominant primordial beast who had made his kill and found it good.".

questions.prompt: London compares Buck’s excitement in the chase to that of an artist and a soldier. What does he mean by an “ecstasy” that comes as “a complete forgetfulness that one is alive”?
facilitatorNotes: At the peak of intensity a creature stops being self-aware and is wholly absorbed. Students may find the soldier comparison disturbing, since it presents violence and art as similar intensities.
evidence: There is an ecstasy that marks the summit of life, and beyond which life cannot rise.
this ecstasy comes when one is most alive, and it comes as a complete forgetfulness that one is alive

questions.prompt: How does Spitz’s way of hunting the rabbit differ from Buck’s, and how does that difference reappear in the fight?
facilitatorNotes: Spitz cuts across the bend while Buck runs flat out; Spitz is cool and practised, defending before attacking, while Buck at first rushes. Some students will argue that Buck wins by learning a version of Spitz’s coolness.
evidence: But Spitz, cold and calculating even in his supreme moods,
Bitter rage was his, but never blind rage.

questions.prompt: What quality, according to the narrator, lets Buck win, and what does he actually do?
facilitatorNotes: He feints the shoulder trick and attacks Spitz’s legs. “Imagination” here means inventive strategy; students may debate whether calling it “greatness” celebrates violence.
evidence: But Buck possessed a quality that made for greatness—imagination.

questions.prompt: The silent circle of dogs appears several times. How does its meaning change from the start of the fight to the end?
facilitatorNotes: It begins as an audience, becomes a threat to whichever dog falls, and finally closes on Spitz, as the pack once closed on Curly. The last phrase, that Buck “found it good,” can be read as triumph or as chilling.
evidence: They, too, were silent, their eyes only gleaming
Only this time he was the one who was beaten.

days.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: Claiming the lead
days.challenge: Distinguish the handlers’ interpretation of resistance from Buck’s intended demand.
days.focus: Negotiation, authority and the costs of restored order.
days.context: The night before, Buck killed Spitz in a fight to the death. In the morning the drivers find Spitz gone and must choose a new lead dog. This passage begins the chapter titled “Who Has Won to Mastership.”
days.contentNote: The drivers discuss the fatal fight; clubs are threatened and Buck forcefully disciplines other dogs. François’s dialect is the author’s period representation.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 4; begins ""EH? Wot I say? I spik true w'en I say dat Buck two devils.""; ends "o, nevaire! Heem worth one t'ousan' dollair, by Gar! Eh? Wot you say, Perrault?"".

questions.prompt: Why does putting down the club once fail, but later succeed?
facilitatorNotes: The first time Buck is still offered his old job. The second time the lead position is open, so the gesture removes the remaining threat.
evidence: There was no place for Buck save at the front.

questions.prompt: How does time pressure give Buck bargaining power?
facilitatorNotes: He refuses to flee permanently or submit; every delay costs the couriers progress, eventually making concession useful.
evidence: Time was flying

questions.prompt: Is the team’s restored solidarity described as kindness?
facilitatorNotes: It is effective coordination secured partly through force. Students may admire competence while questioning the means; use both the improved teamwork and punishment.
evidence: once more the dogs leaped as one dog in the traces

days.title: The Lost World — excerpt: A hidden waterway
days.challenge: Track a concealed entrance through precise colour cues and extended imagery.
days.focus: Discovery depends on attention, while beauty coexists with uncertainty.
days.context: The expedition is following Challenger toward the plateau. A palm marks the position of a stream entrance concealed by riverside growth.
days.contentNote: Lord John dismisses Indigenous beliefs in condescending language. The guide’s knowledge and warning should not be treated as disproved by the explorers’ confidence.

excerpt.locator: Hodder and Stoughton 1912 scan-backed Wikisource text, Chapter 8, transcribed paragraphs 24–31; begins "\"It is surely an Assai palm,\" said Summerlee."; ends "ankets, and the rest—and, shouldering our packages, we set forth upon the more laborious stage of our journey.".

questions.prompt: What small visual difference reveals an opening where no obvious gap exists?
facilitatorNotes: Light-green rushes replace darker undergrowth. The detail makes close observation, not a spectacular landmark, essential to entry.
evidence: light-green rushes instead of dark-green undergrowth

questions.prompt: What is the effect of comparing the river to crystal, glass and an iceberg?
facilitatorNotes: The comparisons layer clarity, stillness and colour; an iceberg is strikingly remote from the tropical setting. Responses may differ on which comparison most strongly creates wonder.
evidence: green as the edge of an iceberg

questions.prompt: Why must the party change its method of travel despite the stream’s beauty?
facilitatorNotes: The water becomes too shallow, and repeated groundings supply practical evidence. They hide the canoes and mark a tree before carrying supplies onward.
evidence: the stream was rapidly growing more shallow

days.title: Strange fits of passion have I known
days.challenge: Read once for physical movement, once for the speaker’s attention, and once for the unsupported fear that arrives at the end.
days.focus: The difference between an observed event and an emotionally persuasive association.
days.context: A lover rides toward Lucy’s cottage while watching the moon. The poem tells a fear that enters his mind; it does not report the discovery of a death.
days.contentNote: The final stanza imagines a loved one’s death.

excerpt.locator: Strange fits of passion have I known, complete individual poem in volume2; HTML poem-text column beginning “Strange fits of passion have I known:” and ending “"If Lucy should be dead!"”; variant, annotation and line-number columns excluded.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker tell the experience only in a lover’s ear?
facilitatorNotes: He expects emotional recognition from someone who knows a similar vulnerability. The restricted audience anticipates a feeling that may seem unreasonable outside that experience.
evidence: in the Lover's ear alone

questions.prompt: How do the horse’s continuing steps and the moon’s sudden disappearance create different rhythms?
facilitatorNotes: Repeated physical movement makes the abrupt visual loss stand out. The contrast prepares the leap from a gradual approach to a shocking imagined possibility.
evidence: At once, the bright moon dropped.

questions.prompt: Which fact supports the final fear, and which part comes entirely from the speaker’s mind?
facilitatorNotes: Only the moon has disappeared behind the roof. Lucy’s death is a conditional thought, not something the speaker observes; the poem exposes an association without proving it.
evidence: If Lucy should be dead!

days.title: Ivanhoe: A Monk and a Warrior
days.challenge: Infer temperament from selected details of dress, movement, and expression.
days.focus: Contradictions between religious roles and worldly display.
days.context: Two prominent riders approach the men in the forest.
days.contentNote: This historical novel imagines twelfth-century England through nineteenth-century assumptions. Its national, religious, racial, and class generalizations are perspectives to examine, not reliable descriptions of whole peoples. Historical insults and threats appear in the original text.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, Chapter II, paragraphs 2–6 of the Wikisource transcription; opens “Notwithstanding the occasional exhortation and chiding of his companio”; closes “g and double-edged dagger, which was the only offensive weapon about his person.”.

questions.prompt: How does the churchman’s clothing complicate the narrator’s claim that it resembles a religious habit?
facilitatorNotes: Expensive fabric and ornament turn an outward sign of discipline into luxury. The description makes institutional appearance and personal appetite pull apart.
evidence: materials much finer

questions.prompt: What does the churchman’s ability to make his face solemn suggest about judging his character?
facilitatorNotes: The respectable exterior can cover inward feelings without proving that those feelings have changed. Facial description becomes an interpretation of self-presentation.
evidence: a ready command over his countenance

questions.prompt: How does the second rider’s armor change the meaning of his monk-like robe?
facilitatorNotes: Armor underneath reveals a military identity beneath religious form; his white cross joins devotion with force. The narrator stresses a more dangerous temperament than the churchman’s ease.
evidence: a shirt, namely, of linked mail

days.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: Two fires
days.challenge: Track the movement between routine work, remembered home and an imagined ancestral scene.
days.focus: Layered memory and the limits of care.
days.context: After a record run, Buck’s team has changed handlers and now hauls heavy mail loads.
days.contentNote: A now-offensive mixed-ancestry label appears. Animal deaths are briefly recalled; the ancestral vision reflects speculative period ideas.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 4; begins "A Scotch half-breed took charge of him and his mates, and in"; ends "sourer than ever, and Sol-leks was unapproachable, blind side or other side.".

questions.prompt: Why does the mail train’s regularity matter before the dream begins?
facilitatorNotes: The fixed schedule makes the sudden imaginative journey away from ordinary time more striking.
evidence: operating with machine-like regularity

questions.prompt: How do the two fires connect present Buck with the other man?
facilitatorNotes: The same posture and flames become a bridge between a current camp and a remote imagined past; the cook’s voice reverses the transition.
evidence: the flames were of another fire

questions.prompt: Why end with the dogs losing strength despite being fed first?
facilitatorNotes: Attentive individuals cannot erase the burden of too much work and too little rest. The detail prevents an easy equation of care with adequate conditions.
evidence: Still, their strength went down.

days.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: Dave in the traces
days.challenge: Interpret an animal’s actions as the narrator does, and weigh the men’s decision.
days.focus: Pride in work, mercy and death on the trail.
days.context: Buck now leads the team, but the dogs have been handed to a mail service and haul heavy loads under a new driver. The long run has worn them down.
days.contentNote: A sick dog suffers, is allowed to work until he collapses, and is shot out of sight. The narrator uses a now-offensive label for a man of mixed ancestry.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 4; begins "But it was Dave who suffered most of all. Something had gone wrong wit"; ends "k knew, and every dog knew, what had taken place behind the belt of river trees.".

questions.prompt: Why does Dave fight to get back into the traces when running free behind the sled would be easier?
facilitatorNotes: Work has become his identity, and being replaced hurts more than pain. Students may see this as noble or as a sign of how completely the dogs have been shaped by their work.
evidence: For the pride of trace and trail was his, and, sick unto death, he could not bear that another dog should do his work.

questions.prompt: The drivers decide it is “a mercy” to let Dave die in the traces. Do you agree with their reasoning?
facilitatorNotes: Both answers are defensible: it honours what Dave seems to want, and it also takes a last day’s work from a suffering animal. The text reports the men’s view without fully endorsing it.
evidence: they held it a mercy, since Dave was to die anyway, that he should die in the traces, heart-easy and content

questions.prompt: The final paragraph never states what happened to Dave. How does London let the reader and the dogs know?
facilitatorNotes: Short sentences, a single sound, then cheerful bells that contrast with what everyone understands. The understatement makes the moment heavier.
evidence: A revolver-shot rang out.
but Buck knew, and every dog knew, what had taken place behind the belt of river trees

days.title: The Lost World — excerpt: What does the snake prove?
days.challenge: Distinguish a broad claim from the narrower observation that supports it.
days.focus: Proof, disputed assumptions and traces left by earlier travellers.
days.context: The party has reached the plateau’s cliffs but cannot find a way up. Challenger treats White’s drawing as evidence of an earlier ascent; Summerlee remains unconvinced.
days.contentNote: The scene includes forceful grabbing and condescending treatment between colleagues.

excerpt.locator: Hodder and Stoughton 1912 scan-backed Wikisource text, Chapter 9, transcribed paragraphs 17–32; begins "\"There seems to be only one reasonable course,\" said Professor Summerlee. \"If you have explored the east, we s"; ends "h follows him may know the way he has taken. Perhaps we shall come upon some other indications as we proceed.\"".

questions.prompt: Why does Summerlee say Challenger reasons ahead of the facts?
facilitatorNotes: Challenger infers an ascent from a drawing whose authenticity remains disputed. Summerlee accepts the visible plateau without automatically accepting the living monsters.
evidence: There you reason somewhat ahead of the proved facts

questions.prompt: What does the snake establish, and what does it leave unproved?
facilitatorNotes: It establishes animal life at the top, but an ordinary python does not establish prehistoric animals. Challenger celebrates a narrower fact as a victory.
evidence: a very ordinary rock python

questions.prompt: How does the abandoned camp suggest a route rather than simply a previous presence?
facilitatorNotes: Travel debris indicates a visitor; the deliberately nailed wood points west. Distinguish recognising human traces from interpreting one as guidance.
evidence: a sign-post

days.title: She dwelt among the untrodden ways
days.challenge: Reread the twelve lines slowly, testing how each image changes the apparent scale of one person’s importance.
days.focus: Public obscurity, private value, and the turn in the final exclamation.
days.context: This lyric introduces a largely unnoticed young woman named Lucy. Compare the work of the two central images before explaining the ending.
days.contentNote: The poem mourns a death without describing its circumstances.

excerpt.locator: She dwelt among the untrodden ways, complete individual poem in volume2; HTML poem-text column beginning “She dwelt among the untrodden ways” and ending “The difference to me!”; variant, annotation and line-number columns excluded.

questions.prompt: How do a partly hidden violet and a solitary star make Lucy noticeable in different ways?
facilitatorNotes: The flower suggests modest, overlooked beauty close to earth; the single star can dominate attention by being alone. Both avoid measuring value by public recognition.
evidence: A violet by a mossy stone

questions.prompt: Why does the poem repeat the idea of few people knowing or loving her?
facilitatorNotes: It establishes the limited public response against which the speaker’s personal loss will become immense. Obscurity is a social circumstance rather than evidence of lesser worth.
evidence: She lived unknown, and few could know

questions.prompt: What does the poem gain by saying “The difference to me” without describing that difference fully?
facilitatorNotes: The sudden first-person exclamation makes the loss intimate while leaving its magnitude unmeasured. Readers may hear restraint, shock, or an inability to elaborate.
evidence: The difference to me!

days.title: Ivanhoe: The Reputation of a Prior
days.challenge: Separate the narrator’s judgments from the local community’s reasons for approval.
days.focus: How public generosity can protect a powerful person’s reputation.
days.context: The procession includes armed servants and attendants described through the novel’s prejudiced view of foreignness.
days.contentNote: This historical novel imagines twelfth-century England through nineteenth-century assumptions. Its national, religious, racial, and class generalizations are perspectives to examine, not reliable descriptions of whole peoples. Historical insults and threats appear in the original text.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, Chapter II, paragraphs 7–12 of the Wikisource transcription; opens “He rode not a mule, like his companion, but a strong hackney for the r”; closes “gracious, though not probably unintelligible, in the ears of the Saxon peasants.”.

questions.prompt: Why bring a spare horse carrying armor behind the Templar?
facilitatorNotes: His road horse conserves the war-horse’s strength. The equipment makes the journey look like a moving military establishment rather than a modest pilgrimage.
evidence: to save his gallant war-horse

questions.prompt: What makes the prior acceptable to people who know he does not practice severe self-denial?
facilitatorNotes: Hospitality, charity, and an accessible manner outweigh strict discipline in their estimation. This explanation of popularity is not proof that every accusation is true or unimportant.
evidence: He was generous

questions.prompt: How does the procession produce different kinds of recognition in Wamba and Gurth?
facilitatorNotes: The familiar prior can be classified through local reputation, but the unfamiliar armed companion makes interpretation uncertain. Clothing and equipment become clues before conversation begins.
evidence: arrested their attention

days.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: A mountainous load
days.challenge: Infer incompetence from actions, irony and conflicting explanations.
days.focus: Advice that pride prevents people from hearing.
days.context: New owners Hal, Charles and Mercedes prepare to drive the already exhausted team toward Dawson.
days.contentNote: The scene threatens animal abuse and uses gender stereotypes in its satire of the inexperienced owners.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 5; begins "Buck watched them apprehensively as they proceeded to take down the tent"; ends "driving our dogs, and you do what you think best with them.\"".

questions.prompt: What does unpacking the clothes-sack reveal beyond mere untidiness?
facilitatorNotes: No plan coordinates decisions; correction undoes earlier labor. Compare effort with useful method.
evidence: a great deal of effort about their manner, but no businesslike method

questions.prompt: Why do the neighbors ask mild questions instead of giving blunt orders?
facilitatorNotes: Their irony lets readers hear a warning the owners refuse to hear. The apparent politeness contrasts with practical knowledge.
evidence: Think it'll ride?

questions.prompt: How does Mercedes’s final speech undermine her earlier defense of the dogs?
facilitatorNotes: Family loyalty overrides concern after she hears they are exhausted; sentiment does not lead to accepting relevant evidence.
evidence: you do what you think best with them

days.title: The Lost World — excerpt: A tree becomes a bridge
days.challenge: Hold the obstacle in mind while following the delayed disclosure of a plan.
days.focus: Inventiveness, suspense and the distribution of credit.
days.context: The expedition has completed a circuit of the cliffs and found no usable ascent. An isolated pinnacle stands beside the plateau, separated from it by a deep gap.
days.contentNote: Dangerous climbing and tree-felling are fictional action, not practical instructions.

excerpt.locator: Hodder and Stoughton 1912 scan-backed Wikisource text, Chapter 9, transcribed paragraphs 82–108; begins "On the sixth day we completed our first circuit of the cliffs, and found ourselves back at the first camp, bes"; ends "hout a word, shook hands with Professor Challenger, who raised his straw hat and bowed deeply to each in turn.".

questions.prompt: Why does reaching the pinnacle initially seem useless to Malone?
facilitatorNotes: The climb changes their height but not the gap. His comparison of forty feet with forty miles expresses the obstacle’s practical rather than numerical size.
evidence: it might as well have been forty miles

questions.prompt: How does the tree’s description change once Challenger explains the plan?
facilitatorNotes: It shifts from familiar vegetation and support for Malone to an ally and a drawbridge. The same object gains a new function through an altered problem frame.
evidence: This beech tree will be our saviour.

questions.prompt: What does the near fall of the severed trunk add after the idea seems solved?
facilitatorNotes: It shows that execution still has uncertainty. The balancing trunk provides a last moment of suspense before the handshakes.
evidence: for one terrible second we all thought that it was over

days.title: I travelled among unknown men
days.challenge: Follow the address to England, then reread to see how a public declaration becomes grounded in intimate places and actions.
days.focus: The relation between attachment to a country and memory of a person.
days.context: The speaker addresses England after traveling abroad. The lyric gradually introduces Lucy as part of what makes home meaningful.
days.contentNote: The speaker expresses a personal patriotic attachment, not proof that one country or people is superior; the ending implies loss.

excerpt.locator: I travelled among unknown men, complete individual poem in volume2; HTML poem-text column beginning “I travelled among unknown men,” and ending “That Lucy's eyes surveyed.”; variant, annotation and line-number columns excluded.

questions.prompt: Why does travel among strangers reveal a love the speaker had not recognized at home?
facilitatorNotes: Distance supplies a comparison and makes a previously familiar attachment noticeable. The first stanza presents discovery of his own feeling rather than a description of foreign people.
evidence: Nor, England! did I know till then

questions.prompt: How does Lucy turning a wheel beside a fire change the scale of the address to England?
facilitatorNotes: The national name becomes attached to domestic work, warmth, and a particular beloved person. The abstract declaration gains specific emotional grounds.
evidence: Beside an English fire

questions.prompt: What makes the final green field more than another attractive landscape?
facilitatorNotes: It is the last one Lucy saw, making place inseparable from memory and mortality. The possessive address to England gathers both happiness and loss into the idea of home.
evidence: the last green field

days.title: Ivanhoe: Directions and Defiance
days.challenge: Track how answers can resist a demand while appearing to obey it.
days.focus: Wit, force, and competing ideas of hospitality.
days.context: The prior asks for lodging; his armed companion becomes impatient with the servants’ replies.
days.contentNote: This historical novel imagines twelfth-century England through nineteenth-century assumptions. Its national, religious, racial, and class generalizations are perspectives to examine, not reliable descriptions of whole peoples. Historical insults and threats appear in the original text.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, Chapter II, paragraphs 13–36 of the Wikisource transcription; opens “"I asked you, my children," said the Prior, raising his voice, and usi”; closes “s military monk. But, like good servants, let us hear and see, and say nothing."”.

questions.prompt: How does Wamba undermine the prior’s claim to be one of the humblest servants of the Church?
facilitatorNotes: His private remark measures the claim against worldly rank and display. The respectful language of the request does not match the authority with which it is delivered.
evidence: Two of the humblest servants

questions.prompt: Why does Gurth object to guests demanding help at an inconvenient hour?
facilitatorNotes: He distinguishes a favor freely offered from a right forcibly claimed. The soldier’s threat demonstrates exactly the attitude Gurth resists.
evidence: demand as a right

days.title: Water Borders — the weeping mountain

days.focus: Mystery as an effect of partial access rather than absence of natural processes.

evidence: will not by me who love them

facilitatorNotes: The visible effort is slight and controlled even during swift descent; repose describes its manner, not absence of motion.

questions.prompt: Where does the account of escaping crows become advice about human conflict?
facilitatorNotes: Calling an opponent a braggart and suggesting imitation turns the climbing spiral into a model of rising beyond a quarrel.

questions.prompt: Why does the disappearing hawk work as the final image of the season?
facilitatorNotes: Its peaceful departure gathers the surrounding account of migrating birds into one visible movement toward the horizon.
evidence: a symbol of the closing season

days.title: A slumber did my spirit seal
days.challenge: Read the two stanzas several times, noticing tense, negation, and the difference between bodily stillness and planetary movement.
days.focus: A change in consciousness compressed into eight lines.
days.context: The first stanza remembers the speaker’s earlier state of mind; the second describes the beloved’s present condition. Give the pauses between the stanzas time to work.
days.contentNote: The poem concerns death and the body’s place in the natural world.

questions.prompt: Who is sealed by slumber in the opening, and why does that matter?
facilitatorNotes: It is the speaker’s spirit, not necessarily a literal sleeper. The phrase can describe an unthinking confidence that the beloved was beyond aging.

questions.prompt: How does “now” divide the poem’s understanding of time?
facilitatorNotes: The remembered lack of fear gives way to a present condition without motion, hearing, or sight. The word marks a change the first stanza had failed to imagine.
evidence: No motion has she now, no force

questions.prompt: How can the second stanza deny motion and still say she is rolled around with the earth?
facilitatorNotes: Individual agency and sensation have ended, while movement on a planetary scale continues. Whether that sounds consoling or chilling depends on the reading, but both must account for the same final image.
evidence: With rocks, and stones, and trees.

days.title: A Christmas Carol — Stave Three: beyond the warm houses

evidence: they all joined in the chorus

questions.prompt: What can the sailors share even when those they love are far away?
facilitatorNotes: Memory, kinder words, and confidence in being remembered create connection across physical distance.
evidence: had known that they delighted to remember him

questions.prompt: Why does elevation complicate an explanation of bird distribution based only on latitude?

facilitatorNotes: He seeks attention, knowledge, and pleasure in birdsong, using the vocabulary of gathering to describe an experience rather than another commodity.

days.title: Lucy Gray

facilitatorNotes: She has reason to think there is still time. The storm’s early arrival defeats an expectation based on ordinary timekeeping, without proving that she could foresee the danger.
evidence: The storm came on before its time

questions.prompt: Why does the poem spend several stanzas following the footprints one by one?
facilitatorNotes: The precise route briefly restores hope by offering material evidence after a fruitless search. The sudden end of the marks at the bridge is therefore more devastating.

facilitatorNotes: Its appearance prompts the speaker’s own memory of childhood and family. The metaphor locates historical feeling in an encounter rather than in a written account.

questions.prompt: How can a gay creature bring a solemn image to the heart?
facilitatorNotes: The lively butterfly revives a family world separated from the present by time. Joy in recognition and gravity about what has passed can coexist.

facilitatorNotes: He remembers energetic pursuit and possession; she remembers possible harm. The affectionate comparison lets the adult reassess his younger impulse without denying its pleasure.
evidence: feared to brush

he sometimes came out with his guess quite loud, and very often guessed right

facilitatorNotes: The Spirit ages because its life is this one Christmas present; the aging dramatizes that the present passes and cannot be recovered. Students may connect it with urgency: what is not done now cannot be done later.

It ends to-night.

questions.prompt: The Spirit says the two children are “Man’s.” What does it mean by naming them Ignorance and Want, and why does it warn most of all about the boy?
facilitatorNotes: They personify conditions society creates: lack of education and poverty. Ignorance is more dangerous because it keeps people from understanding and changing harm. evidence: This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want.
most of all beware this boy

facilitatorNotes: In Stave One Scrooge used these questions to refuse charity. Now they expose his indifference at the moment he finally feels concern. Students may debate whether the Spirit is being cruel or teaching through shock.
evidence: Are there no prisons?
turning on him for the last time with his own words

days.contentNote: The scene describes stealing from a dead man’s room and body, including his bed-curtains and burial shirt. It is grim but not graphic.

why wasn't he natural in his lifetime?

facilitatorNotes: Even the body’s last dignity has been traded, and the comic bargaining makes it more chilling. A defensible alternative sees the thefts as survival by very poor people, with the horror belonging partly to Scrooge’s point of view.

facilitatorNotes: He recognizes a resemblance in way of life but not that the man is himself; the reader may already suspect it. Students can argue that he half-sees and refuses to see.

evidence: We may sleep to-night with light hearts, Caroline!
The only emotion that the Ghost could show him, caused by the event, was one of pleasure.

days.title: A Christmas Carol — Stave Four: the Cratchits’ quiet house
days.challenge: Notice how silence, small actions and broken sentences convey a grief that no one names at first.
days.focus: Restraint and indirection in a scene of mourning.
days.context: Scrooge begs the Ghost for “some tenderness connected with a death.” It brings him again to Bob Cratchit’s house, which he visited on Christmas Day with the Ghost of Christmas Present.
days.contentNote: The Cratchit family mourns the death of Tiny Tim, a young disabled child.

excerpt.locator: PG 19337, dated 1905 edition; Stave Four: the Cratchits’ quiet house; narrative paragraphs 574–610; begins ""Let me see some tenderness connected with a death," said Scrooge; "or"; ends " and himself shook hands. Spirit of Tiny Tim, thy childish essence was from God!".

questions.prompt: Tiny Tim’s death is not announced directly at first. Which details let the reader understand it before it is stated?
facilitatorNotes: The silent children, the Bible verse about a child, the mother’s remark that “the colour hurts my eyes” over her sewing, and Peter’s comment that his father walks more slowly. The indirectness lets the reader discover the loss as Scrooge does.
evidence: The noisy little Cratchits were as still as statues in one corner
The colour? Ah, poor Tiny Tim!

questions.prompt: Mrs. Cratchit says Tim “was very light to carry” and “no trouble.” What is she doing for her children, and for herself, by speaking this way?
facilitatorNotes: She steadies her voice to protect the family and to honour Bob’s love for the boy; the repeated “no trouble” shows feeling pressing through. Students may read it as her own consolation as well.
evidence: But he was very light to carry,
and his father loved him so, that it was no trouble: no trouble.

questions.prompt: How does Bob’s visit to the room upstairs change him, and what does the narrator suggest about grief?
facilitatorNotes: Sitting by the child lets him accept the loss, so grief appears as love that can coexist with happiness. Some readers find “quite happy” sentimental or unconvincing; that judgment is open to argument.
evidence: He was reconciled to what had happened, and went down again quite happy.

questions.prompt: Bob says remembering Tim will keep them from quarrelling. Compare this response to a death with the reactions to the dead man in the earlier scenes.
facilitatorNotes: Tim’s memory binds his family together; the other man’s death led to theft and relief. The contrast answers Scrooge’s request for tenderness and judges two kinds of life.
evidence: we shall not quarrel easily among ourselves, and forget poor Tiny Tim in doing it
Spirit of Tiny Tim, thy childish essence was from God!

days.title: A Christmas Carol — Stave Four: the neglected grave
days.challenge: Read a climax in which a question about the future becomes an argument about whether change is possible.
days.focus: The difference between shadows of what “Will be” and what “May be.”
days.context: After the Cratchits’ grief, Scrooge asks the Ghost who the dead man was. The Spirit hurries him through the business streets past his own office. Stave Four ends with this passage.
days.contentNote: Scrooge kneels in terror at a grave; the scene is frightening but not violent.

excerpt.locator: PG 19337, dated 1905 edition; Stave Four: the neglected grave; narrative paragraphs 611–636; begins ""Spectre," said Scrooge, "something informs me that our parting moment"; ends "hantom's hood and dress. It shrunk, collapsed, and dwindled down into a bedpost.".

questions.prompt: Why does the Spirit point away from Scrooge’s office, and what does Scrooge find when he looks in?
facilitatorNotes: His place has been taken by someone else, a hint that he is gone. Scrooge still hopes to see a changed future self.
evidence: It was an office still, but not his.
the figure in the chair was not himself

questions.prompt: Scrooge calls the churchyard “a worthy place” twice. What makes it worthy of the dead man, according to its description?
facilitatorNotes: It is crowded, overgrown and neglected, matching the life of a man no one cared for. The repetition is bitter irony; some students may read it as Scrooge’s dawning recognition.
evidence: the growth of vegetation's death, not life
A worthy place!

questions.prompt: Before reading the stone, Scrooge asks whether these are shadows of things that “Will be” or that “May be only.” Why does that question matter so much to him and to the story?
facilitatorNotes: If the future is fixed, change is pointless; if it is only possible, he can still act. The whole book depends on the second answer, and the Ghost’s silence keeps the tension.
evidence: Are these the shadows of the things that Will be, or are they shadows of the things that May be only?
But if the courses be departed from, the ends will change.

questions.prompt: What signs show the Spirit’s response to Scrooge’s promises, and how does the vision end?
facilitatorNotes: The trembling hand suggests mercy without words. The Spirit’s shrinking into a bedpost returns Scrooge to his room and leaves open whether the visions were dream or reality; both readings are defensible.
evidence: For the first time the hand appeared to shake.
It shrunk, collapsed, and dwindled down into a bedpost.

days.title: A Christmas Carol — Stave Five: time to make amends
days.challenge: Connect repeated objects and expressions with a changed emotional meaning.
days.focus: The shift from private revelation to an immediate generous act.
days.context: Stave Five begins. At the neglected grave that bore his own name, Scrooge begged the Spirit to let him change the future, and the Phantom dwindled into a bedpost. He wakes in his room on Christmas morning.

excerpt.locator: PG 19337, dated 1905 edition; Stave Five: time to make amends; narrative paragraphs 637–671; begins "Yes! and the bedpost was his own. The bed was his own, the room was his own. Best and happiest of all, the Tim"; ends " cut the end of his nose off, he would have put a piece of sticking-plaster over it, and been quite satisfied.".

questions.prompt: Why is time the most valuable possession named in the opening paragraph?
facilitatorNotes: Being alive still gives him an opportunity to repair conduct; room and bed matter less than the chance to act.
evidence: the Time before him was his own

questions.prompt: How do the bells and door knocker acquire a different meaning?
facilitatorNotes: Objects associated with fear now invite delight and affection, making familiar surroundings register an inward change.
evidence: I shall love it as long as I live

questions.prompt: What makes the turkey gift more than an excited declaration of good intentions?
facilitatorNotes: He arranges its purchase and delivery and pays the necessary costs; the new feeling takes a practical form while remaining anonymous to Bob.
evidence: He shan't know

days.title: A Christmas Carol — Stave Five: a change sustained
days.challenge: Distinguish promises, immediate gestures, and the narrator’s account of later conduct.
days.focus: A comic resolution tested by material support and renewed relationships.
days.context: Scrooge goes out to repair his earlier refusals, visits Fred, and returns to work the next morning.
days.contentNote: The comic scene uses a historical image of restraint associated with mental illness. The ending also returns to a Christian blessing.

excerpt.locator: PG 19337, dated 1905 edition; Stave Five: a change sustained; narrative paragraphs 672–707; begins "He dressed himself \"all in his best,\" and at last got out into the streets. The people were by this time pouri"; ends "knowledge. May that be truly said of us, and all of us! And so, as Tiny Tim observed, God bless Us, Every One!".

questions.prompt: What does including “back-payments” in the donation reveal about Scrooge’s understanding of the past?
facilitatorNotes: He recognizes accumulated omissions rather than treating one generous day as disconnected from earlier conduct.
evidence: A great many back-payments

questions.prompt: How does the scene with late-arriving Bob first repeat and then reverse the old office pattern?
facilitatorNotes: Scrooge feigns anger about timekeeping, then announces a raise, family help, and a larger fire. The joke depends on Bob’s well-founded expectation of punishment.
evidence: I am about to raise your salary

questions.prompt: What evidence does the ending supply that the change lasts beyond this morning?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator explicitly reports that he fulfilled and exceeded his word, supported Tiny Tim, and became a good friend and employer. This retrospective account extends the resolution beyond intention.
evidence: Scrooge was better than his word

days.title: Nurslings of the Sky — studying a storm
days.challenge: Distinguish sensory description, practical inference, and a spiritual interpretation of weather.
days.focus: Familiarity, apparent intention, and the limits of a storm-watcher’s confidence.
days.context: Austin contrasts storms on open plains with storms watched among mountains.
days.contentNote: Austin’s confident safety claims are historical rhetoric, not modern weather or mountain-safety advice. The excerpt describes floods and invokes a religious interpretation of nature.

excerpt.locator: Nurslings of the Sky — studying a storm; begins “Choose a hill country for storms. There all the business of the weather is carried on”; ends “or a dull lake pitted by the glancing drops, dissolving as it drives. Such rains relieve like tears.”.

questions.prompt: Why does visibility matter to the contrast between plains and hills?
facilitatorNotes: She argues that seeing clouds and knowing routes and warnings makes a storm intelligible; the hidden approach on plains increases fear.
evidence: added terror of viewlessness

questions.prompt: What do the flooded settlements contribute to her argument about reading a landscape?
facilitatorNotes: Building in a wash or below a steep slope ignores visible routes of water or snow. Her allocation of fault remains a judgment, not proof that all disasters are predictable.
evidence: the fault of neither the water nor the snow

questions.prompt: Where does she go beyond weather measurement into a claim about meaning?
facilitatorNotes: The Spirit and her criticism of the Weather Bureau interpret storms spiritually. Readers can distinguish the sensory observations from the belief she attaches to them.
evidence: sense of presence and intention

days.title: In the Hemlocks — the partridge’s hidden family
days.challenge: Follow a sequence of sounds and silences while questioning purpose attributed to development.
days.focus: Behavioral evidence and the effect of the observer’s presence.
days.context: A walk through the woods brings Burroughs near a brood of young partridges.
days.contentNote: The ending mentions obtaining a shot at a bird. The historical account is not an invitation to approach nests or hunt; its explanation of drumming should be treated as the author’s account.

excerpt.locator: In the Hemlocks — the partridge’s hidden family; begins “I pass on through the old Barkpeeling, now threading an obscure cow-path or an overgr”; ends “ he stands as immovable as a knot, allowing you a good view and a good shot, if you are a sportsman.”.

questions.prompt: What comparison explains why the sandpiper need not fly as early as the partridge?
facilitatorNotes: The sandpiper can escape through water; different escape routes make early wing development seem less urgent in the comparison.
evidence: taking to the water

questions.prompt: How does the observer’s movement change what he can hear?
facilitatorNotes: Hidden listening reveals the mother’s gathering call and responses; stepping out makes the family silent, showing that observation can alter behavior.
evidence: all sounds instantly cease

questions.prompt: What details distinguish the reported drumming from the simple image of beating a log?
facilitatorNotes: The bird stands erect, accelerates wingbeats, and barely brushes the surface. The description redirects attention toward air and movement rather than only a resonant object.
evidence: barely brush the log

days.title: In the Hemlocks — writing down a chorus
days.challenge: Compare several attempts to represent sounds in writing and notice their limitations.
days.focus: Identification, notation, and the emotional close of a descriptive ramble.
days.context: Burroughs listens to several warblers before leaving the woods at twilight.

excerpt.locator: In the Hemlocks — writing down a chorus; begins “Passing along one of the old Barkpeelers' roads which wander aimlessly about, I am at”; ends “xaltation of sentiment of which music, literature, and religion are but the faint types and symbols.”.

questions.prompt: Why is having food in its beak suggestive but insufficient evidence for the mourning warbler’s nest location?
facilitatorNotes: It suggests feeding young but the bird avoids revealing where; observation supports a likely activity without locating its destination.
evidence: carefully avoids betraying

questions.prompt: What can straight lines and altered marks represent in a song that ordinary bird names cannot?
facilitatorNotes: The notation attempts to show pitch, repeated notes, and changed inflection. It communicates a pattern, though readers still lack the actual timbre.
evidence: the tone and inflection are changed

questions.prompt: How does the final pause differ from the preceding catalogue of markings and songs?
facilitatorNotes: Identification gives way to a personal experience of exaltation; twilight and the hermit’s song culminate the excursion rather than add one more species fact.
evidence: the hush and stillness of twilight

days.title: Adirondac — expectation and familiar voices
days.challenge: Assess an expectation against the limited observations of one journey and season.
days.focus: How familiarity can become a discovery in an unfamiliar place.
days.context: Burroughs recalls the beginning of an 1863 visit to the Adirondacks.

excerpt.locator: Adirondac — expectation and familiar voices; begins “When I went to the Adirondacs, which was in the summer of 1863, I was in the first fl”; ends “was by the Boreas River in the deep forest. It was like the voice of an old friend speaking my name.”.

questions.prompt: What expectation about remote woods does the opening challenge?
facilitatorNotes: Distance and apparent wildness do not guarantee more novel birds; he finds many familiar species near settlements and clearings.
evidence: one is disappointed

questions.prompt: How does the white-throated sparrow both satisfy and frustrate his search?
facilitatorNotes: It offers a new, elusive song to identify, but he imagines that the phrase stops just before a satisfying completion.
evidence: ends when it seems only to have begun

questions.prompt: Why does the August timing qualify any conclusion about how musical these woods are?
facilitatorNotes: Molting birds sing only briefly, so the journey samples a quiet season rather than the full range of annual song.
evidence: the birds were all moulting

days.title: My heart leaps up when I behold
days.challenge: Read the short poem aloud repeatedly, stressing different words in its central paradox and testing which interpretation fits all nine lines.
days.focus: Continuity of feeling across a lifetime and the force of a paradox.
days.context: A rainbow makes the speaker connect childhood, adulthood, and hoped-for old age. Spend the reading time on repeated oral readings and a paraphrase of the central paradox before discussing it.
days.contentNote: “Or let me die” is an emphatic poetic expression of the value the speaker places on wonder.

excerpt.locator: My heart leaps up when I behold, complete individual poem in volume2; HTML poem-text column beginning “My heart leaps up when I behold” and ending “Bound each to each by natural piety.”; variant, annotation and line-number columns excluded.

questions.prompt: How do “So was,” “So is,” and “So be” give the poem a structure larger than the single rainbow?
facilitatorNotes: The sequence moves from memory through present experience to a wish for the future. The last stage is desired continuity, not a prediction already proven.
evidence: So be it when I shall grow old

questions.prompt: In what sense can the Child be father of the Man without reversing literal family relationships?
facilitatorNotes: The adult’s capacity for wonder grows from childhood experience, so the earlier self helps form the later one. Other readings should explain why the surrounding lines stress enduring response.
evidence: The Child is father of the Man

questions.prompt: What does binding days together add to simply enjoying separate rainbows?
facilitatorNotes: The closing wish values a sustained relation to the natural world across time. “Natural piety” can suggest reverent loyalty or devotion without requiring readers to supply a particular doctrine.
evidence: Bound each to each by natural piety.

days.title: Nurslings of the Sky — the first snow
days.challenge: Track a sequence of small signals before the visually dominant event arrives.
days.focus: Anticipation built from sound, stillness, and animal movement.
days.context: Austin describes early winter storms and then the different behavior of later, heavier snows.
days.contentNote: The passage mentions hungry or weakened wild animals in deep snow. It is a literary weather account, not an outdoor-safety guide.

excerpt.locator: Nurslings of the Sky — the first snow; begins “The great snows that come at the beginning of winter, before there is yet any snow ex”; ends “ and heavy they spread over the young firs in green-ribbed tents wherein harbor winter loving birds.”.

questions.prompt: How do the creek and trees make the storm perceptible before snow falls?
facilitatorNotes: Creaking, a changing water note, and unusual stillness prepare the observer through sound and movement rather than a first visible flake.
evidence: waiting stillness

questions.prompt: How do first and later snows differ in the passage?
facilitatorNotes: Early snow is wet and clogging, while later snow is fine and dry enough to be swept into banners and drifts.
evidence: mere ice granules

questions.prompt: What sequence allows the silver fir to bear and release a load?
facilitatorNotes: Branches droop toward the trunk, shed snow when overloaded, and recover, after which accumulation begins again.
evidence: the boughs recover

days.title: The Time Machine — excerpt: A fourth dimension at dinner
days.challenge: Follow an argument by analogy while noticing the social performance around it.
days.focus: Scientific persuasion inside a comfortable drawing room.
days.context: An unnamed narrator recalls a dinner at which an inventor proposes that time is a fourth dimension. The argument belongs to a speculative novel, not a physics lesson.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 1; begins "The Time Traveller (for so it will be convenient to speak of"; ends "line, and that line, therefore, we must conclude was along the Time-Dimension.\"".

questions.prompt: Why describe the chairs and relaxed dinner atmosphere before the geometric argument?
facilitatorNotes: Comfort and lazy admiration contrast with the precision the claim needs; the narrator subtly limits the reliability of the discussion.
evidence: free of the trammels of precision

questions.prompt: How does the “instantaneous cube” change the question Filby thinks he is answering?
facilitatorNotes: Filby thinks about three spatial dimensions; the Traveller adds duration as a condition of a physical object’s existence.
evidence: Can a cube that does not last for any time at all, have a real existence?

questions.prompt: What do the portraits and weather chart make easier to imagine, and what do they not demonstrate?
facilitatorNotes: They represent change over time spatially, making duration comprehensible. They do not themselves prove a machine can move through time.
evidence: sections, as it were

days.title: Nurslings of the Sky — the wind and the weather chart
days.challenge: Evaluate an observer’s limited experience while tracing a shift from danger to reflection.
days.focus: The difference between useful classification and a felt interpretation of the sky.
days.context: The essay closes with desert winds and a reflection on studying clouds.
days.contentNote: The passage includes patronizing historical generalizations about Indigenous knowledge and describes sheep lost in a sandstorm. It is not advice for exposure to desert winds.

excerpt.locator: Nurslings of the Sky — the wind and the weather chart; begins “All storms of desert hills, except wind storms, are impotent. East and east of the Si”; ends “d drift over Waban and the spray of your garden hose. And not necessarily then do you live up to it.”.

questions.prompt: How do the sheltered hawks challenge their usual image as masters of the air?
facilitatorNotes: They are grounded and afraid to spread feathers; the wind temporarily removes the advantage of flight.
evidence: not daring to spread a feather

questions.prompt: Why must “I have never heard” be read more cautiously than a universal claim that wind harms no other animals?
facilitatorNotes: It reports the limits of her information, not a systematic survey; the vivid examples do not establish all possible effects.
evidence: I have never heard

questions.prompt: What does the comparison of a mountain rainbow with a garden hose ask readers to recognize?
facilitatorNotes: The same phenomenon spans grand and ordinary settings. Austin asks for experiential recognition beyond names and crop forecasts, without making the practical information useless.
evidence: the same rainbow

days.title: The Time Machine — excerpt: The vanishing model
days.challenge: Separate reported observation from proposed explanation.
days.focus: Witnesses, performance and the limits of a demonstration.
days.context: The Traveller produces a small model after arguing that a machine might move through time.
days.contentNote: Mild profanity and tobacco use appear in the period dinner scene.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 2; begins "The thing the Time Traveller held in his hand was a glittering"; ends "Man; \"but wait until to-morrow. Wait for the common-sense of the morning.\"".

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator map everyone’s position and count the lights?
facilitatorNotes: He anticipates a trick explanation and presents conditions favorable to observation; detail supports his credibility without making him infallible.
evidence: the room was brilliantly illuminated

questions.prompt: What does the Psychologist’s finger establish more firmly than the Traveller’s own finger would?
facilitatorNotes: A guest performs the trigger, reducing one possible sleight of hand. It still does not establish where the vanished object went.
evidence: the Psychologist himself who sent forth the model

questions.prompt: How does the Medical Man’s final comment differ from the Psychologist’s quick explanation?
facilitatorNotes: He postpones judgment until excitement fades, whereas the Psychologist supplies a plausible analogy immediately. Both respond to limited evidence.
evidence: the common-sense of the morning

days.title: Ivanhoe: A Wager over Beauty
days.challenge: Read private speech as evidence that revises the public performance.
days.focus: The limits of practical restraint in the prior’s advice.
days.context: Alone with the Templar, the prior explains Cedric’s household and warns his companion about provoking its master.
days.contentNote: This historical novel imagines twelfth-century England through nineteenth-century assumptions. Its national, religious, racial, and class generalizations are perspectives to examine, not reliable descriptions of whole peoples. Historical insults and threats appear in the original text.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, Chapter II, paragraphs 37–47 of the Wikisource transcription; opens “We return to the riders, who had soon left the bondsmen far behind the”; closes “t disgrace. Doubt not that we shall be strong enough to make good our quarters."”.

questions.prompt: What does the Templar’s proposal to beat Gurth into courtesy reveal about his idea of respect?
facilitatorNotes: He treats outward submission obtained by violence as courtesy. His reference to captives extends that coercive idea beyond this encounter.
evidence: beat him into courtesy

questions.prompt: Why is the prior’s warning about Cedric more practical than principled?
facilitatorNotes: He emphasizes danger, local custom, and the risk of losing hospitality. He does not fundamentally reject the Templar’s entitlement to command others.
evidence: every land has its own manners and fashions

questions.prompt: How does the wager reduce Rowena to an object of judgment?
facilitatorNotes: The men assign a stake to her beauty and let the Templar judge it. Her own wishes have no place in their agreement, which sharpens the importance of her later response.
evidence: against ten butts of Chian wine

days.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: Thornton’s camp
days.challenge: Notice how Buck’s refusal, Thornton’s silence and the danger of the ice come together.
days.focus: Judgment, intervention and the turning point of Buck’s life.
days.context: Buck’s new owners, Hal, his sister Mercedes and her husband Charles, know nothing of the North. Through bad planning and cruelty they have starved and overworked the team, and several dogs have died. In spring they stagger into John Thornton’s camp. The chapter ends with this passage.
days.contentNote: Buck is whipped and clubbed nearly to death, and three people and their dogs break through the river ice and drown.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 5; begins "With the dogs falling, Mercedes weeping and riding, Hal swearing innoc"; ends ""You poor devil," said John Thornton, and Buck licked his hand.".

questions.prompt: Thornton gave his advice “in the certainty that it would not be followed.” What does this reveal about him and about Hal?
facilitatorNotes: Thornton is experienced and detached; Hal is arrogant. Students may debate whether Thornton should have tried harder to stop them, especially for Mercedes and Charles.
evidence: He knew the breed, and he gave his advice in the certainty that it would not be followed.
It was idle, he knew, to get between a fool and his folly

questions.prompt: Why does Buck refuse to get up: exhaustion, choice, or something like foresight?
facilitatorNotes: The text layers several causes: exhaustion, a decision, and a “vague feeling of impending doom” about the ice. A strong answer shows how London combines them.
evidence: unlike them, he had made up his mind not to get up
it seemed that he sensed disaster close at hand

questions.prompt: Thornton attacks with “a cry that was inarticulate and more like the cry of an animal.” Why might London describe a man’s action this way here?
facilitatorNotes: It links Thornton with Buck’s world beyond reasoning and shows compassion acting on instinct. Some students may point out that violence is answered with violence.
evidence: uttering a cry that was inarticulate and more like the cry of an animal

questions.prompt: After the sled breaks through the ice, the chapter ends with a look and four words. What do these quiet lines add after the disaster?
facilitatorNotes: Two survivors recognize each other, and “poor devil” is sympathy, not pity from above. Some readers feel the drowning is told too coolly; London’s flat narration is a deliberate choice that students can evaluate.
evidence: The bottom had dropped out of the trail.
You poor devil,

days.title: The Call of the Wild — excerpt: A different kind of master
days.challenge: Compare several relationships without treating every affectionate action as identical.
days.focus: Trust, convalescence and remembered loss.
days.context: John Thornton has rescued Buck from abusive owners. Buck recovers beside Thornton and his dogs Skeet and Nig.
days.contentNote: Injuries and earlier abuse are recalled. Rough play and biting are literary descriptions, not instructions for handling animals.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 6; begins "WHEN John Thornton froze his feet in the previous December, his partners"; ends "he would stand and listen to the sound of his master's breathing.".

questions.prompt: How do Skeet and Nig make recovery a social experience?
facilitatorNotes: Skeet cleans wounds and both dogs welcome him without jealousy; games restore more than physical strength.
evidence: no jealousy toward him

questions.prompt: What distinction separates Thornton’s care from “business expedience”?
facilitatorNotes: His attention is spontaneous and personal, including greetings and conversation, rather than only maintaining working capacity.
evidence: because he could not help it

questions.prompt: Why does the final image of Buck listening outside the tent qualify the joyful account?
facilitatorNotes: Love includes fear of another loss. Prior changes of masters make secure attachment difficult despite good treatment.
evidence: listen to the sound of his master's breathing
