days.focus: Affection as evidence that unsettles dismissive judgment.
days.context: The Traveller rescues an Eloi named Weena and begins to notice both her attachment and her fear.
days.contentNote: Near-drowning, ominous figures and repeated patronizing descriptions of Weena; no graphic injury.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 8; begins "\"That day, too, I made a friend—of a sort. It happened that,"; ends "they were soon destined to take far deadlier possession of my mind.".

questions.prompt: How does Weena’s gift correct one of the Traveller’s expectations?
facilitatorNotes: He expects no gratitude from her people, but a garland made for him establishes personal recognition and generosity.
evidence: In that, however, I was wrong.

questions.prompt: What does “Until it was too late” let the storyteller know that his earlier self does not?
facilitatorNotes: The retrospective voice signals later loss and a failure to understand her importance and fear; students need not guess the exact future event.
evidence: Until it was too late

questions.prompt: Why is the joke about overcrowded ghosts not a satisfying explanation of the white figures?
facilitatorNotes: It relieves unease but does not account for observations; the figures remain linked to earlier sightings and future danger.
evidence: the jest was unsatisfying

days.title: Ivanhoe: Rowena Draws Her Veil
days.challenge: Follow how gesture and changes of subject answer intrusive attention.
days.focus: A woman’s constrained but visible authority within a public gathering.
days.context: Rowena enters the feast; the Templar stares at her, while Cedric and the prior watch the exchange.
days.contentNote: This historical novel imagines twelfth-century England through nineteenth-century assumptions. Its national, religious, racial, and class generalizations are perspectives to examine, not reliable descriptions of whole peoples. Historical insults and threats appear in the original text.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, Chapter IV, paragraphs 24–47 of the Wikisource transcription; opens “When the repast was about to commence, the major-domo, or steward, sud”; closes “d the steward left the banqueting hall to see the commands of his patron obeyed.”.

questions.prompt: Why is drawing the veil an action rather than merely another detail of clothing?
facilitatorNotes: It responds to the Templar’s gaze and controls what he may see. Rowena refuses the terms of the beauty contest the men privately imagined.
evidence: drew with dignity the veil around her face

questions.prompt: How does Rowena redirect the conversation after the Templar’s compliments?
facilitatorNotes: She asks for news from Palestine, shifting from her appearance to information she wants. Dignified phrasing lets her assert a purpose within the rules of courtesy.
evidence: the latest news from Palestine

questions.prompt: How does Wamba’s calculation about truces expose a gap between official promises and events?
facilitatorNotes: Adding three supposedly fifty-year agreements gives him an absurd age. The joke tests ceremonial claims against actual elapsed time.
evidence: three of them in my day

days.title: The Time Machine — excerpt: Another heir to the ages
days.challenge: Separate sensory detail, analogy and inference in a revised account of humanity.
days.focus: A discovery that exposes exclusions in an attractive theory.
days.context: The Traveller has seen pale figures at dawn and heard machinery beneath the wells. He now encounters one in a dark ruin.
days.contentNote: The Traveller dehumanizes the Morlocks in his descriptions. Astronomical and evolutionary proposals here are period fiction, not current scientific conclusions.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 8; begins "\"I think I have said how much hotter than our own was"; ends "I very soon felt that it fell far short of the truth.".

questions.prompt: Which limits does he admit while describing the fleeing figure?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot clearly see its movement or posture, despite vivid impressions; his confidence varies with the kind of claim.
evidence: My impression of it is, of course, imperfect

questions.prompt: Why is “also heir to all the ages” a more significant realization than discovering an unfamiliar animal?
facilitatorNotes: He recognizes shared human descent in a being he finds repellent, breaking the equation of humanity with the beautiful Eloi.
evidence: also heir to all the ages

questions.prompt: What supports the underground-living hypothesis, and what further claim goes beyond those observations?
facilitatorNotes: Pallor, reflective eyes and difficulty in sunlight support the habitat inference. Supposing they produce all Eloi comforts adds an economic explanation.
evidence: The notion was so plausible

days.title: Ivanhoe: A Door Open, a Place Refused
days.challenge: Set an epigraph’s appeal to shared humanity beside the behavior that follows.
days.focus: Formal admission and genuine welcome are different acts.
days.context: A traveler named Isaac seeks shelter. The chapter begins with words from Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice.
days.contentNote: This historical novel imagines twelfth-century England through nineteenth-century assumptions. Its national, religious, racial, and class generalizations are perspectives to examine, not reliable descriptions of whole peoples. Historical insults and threats appear in the original text.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, Chapter V, paragraphs 1–16 of the Wikisource transcription; opens “Hath not a Jew eyes? Hath not a Jew hands, organs, dimensions, senses,”; closes “ most desperate means from the apprehended contamination of his nearer approach.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening appeal to common senses and needs challenge the reception Isaac receives?
facilitatorNotes: The epigraph emphasizes shared human vulnerability; the guests immediately treat religious difference as a reason for contempt. The placement encourages readers to judge their response.
evidence: Hath not a Jew eyes?

questions.prompt: What does Cedric defend when he refuses to let his guests decide who can enter?
facilitatorNotes: He protects his duty and authority as host against their dislike. His permission does not, however, remove his own prejudiced language or ensure that others make room.
evidence: my hospitality must not be bounded by your dislikes

questions.prompt: Why does the scene continue after Isaac is admitted instead of treating admission as its solution?
facilitatorNotes: Everyone can avoid offering a place, leaving him formally sheltered but practically excluded. Physical arrangement reveals the limits of the host’s declaration.
evidence: no one offered to make room for him

days.title: The Time Machine — excerpt: Class divided into species
days.challenge: Distinguish a social warning from a demonstrated history of the imagined future.
days.focus: Extrapolation from Victorian inequality and resistance from new evidence.
days.context: The Traveller calls the daylight people Eloi and the underground people Morlocks. He tries to explain the division using the society he knows.
days.contentNote: The speech includes class prejudice, threatened starvation and speculative biological hierarchy; the story marks its account as uncertain.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 8; begins "\"At first, proceeding from the problems of our own age, it seemed"; ends "was smiling and clapping her hands, while I solemnly burnt a match.".

questions.prompt: How does “birthright in the sky” turn an industrial trend into a moral claim?
facilitatorNotes: Access to daylight sounds like something workers should possess, not a luxury granted by owners. Underground development becomes dispossession.
evidence: Industry had gradually lost its birthright in the sky

questions.prompt: What changes in his meaning of “triumph” compared with his earlier paradise?
facilitatorNotes: Success now benefits an aristocracy at others’ expense; control of nature and control of people become linked.
evidence: a triumph over nature and the fellow-man

questions.prompt: Which questions at the end unsettle the assumption that Eloi are masters?
facilitatorNotes: Their inability to retrieve the machine and terror of darkness do not fit simple continuing control of the Morlocks.
evidence: if the Eloi were masters, could they not restore the machine to me?

days.title: The Time Machine — excerpt: Down the well
days.challenge: Notice how the Traveller admits fear and self-deception before he acts.
days.focus: Courage and curiosity in a descent into the unknown.
days.context: The Traveller has realized that pale, ape-like creatures he calls Morlocks live underground beneath the wells, and he suspects they have taken his Time Machine. This passage begins the chapter titled “The Morlocks.”
days.contentNote: A frightening climb into darkness; the Traveller describes the Morlocks with disgust.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 9; begins ""It may seem odd to you, but it was two days before I could follow up "; ends "utters and tunnels, from which their eyes glared at me in the strangest fashion.".

questions.prompt: Why does the Traveller delay his descent, and how does he later judge his excuse about the Palace of Green Porcelain?
facilitatorNotes: He is afraid, and he admits the excuse was self-deception. That honesty builds his credibility as a narrator; students may connect it with ordinary procrastination.
evidence: my curiosity regarding the Palace of Green Porcelain was a piece of self-deception
Yet I could not face the mystery.

questions.prompt: How does Weena react at the well, and what does the Traveller’s response show about their relationship?
facilitatorNotes: She knows the danger and tries to stop him; he dismisses her, protective yet patronizing. Some students will say she is wiser than he is here.
evidence: Then she gave a most piteous cry
I shook her off, perhaps a little roughly

questions.prompt: Which details of the climb make the descent physically vivid?
facilitatorNotes: The bending bar, aching arms, the thudding machines and the sky shrinking to a small disk with a star visible in daylight all emphasize depth and danger.
evidence: One of the bars bent suddenly under my weight
Glancing upward, I saw the aperture, a small blue disk, in which a star was visible

questions.prompt: He compares the Morlocks’ eyes to “the pupils of the abysmal fishes.” What does this comparison suggest about how they have adapted?
facilitatorNotes: They have adapted to darkness as deep-sea fish have. Wells uses evolutionary reasoning, and the Traveller thinks like a naturalist even when afraid.
evidence: their eyes were abnormally large and sensitive, just as are the pupils of the abysmal fishes

days.title: The Time Machine — excerpt: Four matches in the Underworld
days.challenge: Track how the Traveller’s limited light shapes what he sees and what he can conclude.
days.focus: Evidence glimpsed in the dark, and a narrator’s admitted lack of preparation.
days.context: The Traveller has climbed down a shaft into the Morlocks’ world and been woken in a tunnel by a soft hand touching his face. The chapter ends with this passage.
days.contentNote: The Traveller is seized in darkness by many hands and sees meat on a table, a hint about what the Morlocks eat.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 9; begins ""I tried to call to them, but the language they had was apparently dif"; ends "rs, and the voices of others among the Eloi. Then, for a time, I was insensible.".

questions.prompt: What does the Traveller see on the table in the cavern, and why does he only wonder at the time what animal it came from?
facilitatorNotes: The meat hints that the Morlocks eat the Eloi; he does not yet draw that conclusion, though a reader may. Students can discuss this dramatic irony.
evidence: The Morlocks at any rate were carnivorous!
what large animal could have survived to furnish the red joint I saw

questions.prompt: He says he came with “the absurd assumption” that the future would be far ahead of his own time. What does he regret not bringing, and what does the list show?
facilitatorNotes: Weapons, medicine, tobacco and a camera: a mix of serious and comic regrets that humanizes him. The camera would have given evidence, which matters because his listeners doubt him.
evidence: I had come without arms, without medicine, without anything to smoke
If only I had thought of a Kodak!

questions.prompt: Why are the matches so important, and how does Wells use them to structure the escape?
facilitatorNotes: Light is his only power over the Morlocks, so the dwindling count creates a countdown. Fire returns later in the story.
evidence: four safety matches that still remained to me
I lit my last match . . . and it incontinently went out.

questions.prompt: How does the Traveller describe the Morlocks’ faces, and what does “nauseatingly inhuman” tell us about his perspective?
facilitatorNotes: Disgust shapes his view, yet the Morlocks are descended from humans, which makes “inhuman” ironic. Students may question his objectivity.
evidence: You can scarce imagine how nauseatingly inhuman they looked

days.title: Ivanhoe: A Seat beside the Fire
days.challenge: Track two kinds of distinction: a quiet act of aid and a contest over military reputation.
days.focus: Actions of compassion beside competitive claims of honor.
days.context: Isaac has entered but no one has welcomed him. The Palmer notices his discomfort as the feast’s conversation continues.
days.contentNote: This historical novel imagines twelfth-century England through nineteenth-century assumptions. Its national, religious, racial, and class generalizations are perspectives to examine, not reliable descriptions of whole peoples. Historical insults and threats appear in the original text.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, Chapter V, paragraphs 17–30 of the Wikisource transcription; opens “Probably the same motives which induced Cedric to open his hall to thi”; closes “ Temple—and Sir Brian de Bois-Guilbert well knows the truth of what I tell you."”.

questions.prompt: How does the Palmer’s response supply what Cedric’s order alone failed to provide?
facilitatorNotes: He offers his own place, food, and warmth. Concrete attention meets the traveler’s need more fully than merely allowing him through the door.
evidence: resigned his seat

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator describe the pair as a possible subject for a painter?
facilitatorNotes: The visual contrast brings relief, age, and compassion into one memorable scene. It pauses the social noise to make the overlooked action important.
evidence: Had there been painters

questions.prompt: How does the Palmer’s interruption change his role in the hall?
facilitatorNotes: A quiet, socially marginal observer becomes an assertive witness willing to challenge the Templar’s account. The emphatic word moves him into the public rivalry.
evidence: Second to none,

days.title: The Time Machine — excerpt: Flowers under unfamiliar stars
days.challenge: Follow a shift between immediate danger, deep time and a physical object in the framing scene.
days.focus: Cosmic scale and personal attachment.
days.context: After his escape from the Morlocks’ Underworld, the Traveller seeks a safer place with Weena, aiming for the distant Palace of Green Porcelain.
days.contentNote: Fear and an indirect, non-graphic suggestion that the Morlocks prey on Eloi appear. The passage does not describe an attack.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 10; begins "\"I wandered during the afternoon along the valley of the Thames, but"; ends "I sat down again, took off my shoes, and flung them away.".

questions.prompt: What changes when the narrator interrupts the journey to place flowers on the table?
facilitatorNotes: An object crosses from remembered adventure into the dinner scene, serving as both possible evidence and a trace of Weena’s care.
evidence: silently placed two withered flowers

questions.prompt: Why can stars be comforting when their constellations are unfamiliar?
facilitatorNotes: They retain a sense of continuity and vast order even though time has rearranged familiar patterns; the image of an old friend joins similarity and change.
evidence: like the face of an old friend

questions.prompt: Does viewing human history against the stars permanently remove his fear?
facilitatorNotes: It briefly dwarfs his troubles, but thought returns to the Eloi and sleeping Weena. Philosophical scale cannot erase immediate attachment.
evidence: I looked at little Weena sleeping beside me

days.title: Ivanhoe: The Sixth Knight
days.challenge: Read hesitation and selective detail as clues without assuming an identity the passage has not established.
days.focus: Memory, pride, and the public stakes of a name.
days.context: The Palmer has challenged the Templar’s account of a tournament. Cedric and Rowena listen as he names the victors.
days.contentNote: This historical novel imagines twelfth-century England through nineteenth-century assumptions. Its national, religious, racial, and class generalizations are perspectives to examine, not reliable descriptions of whole peoples. Historical insults and threats appear in the original text.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, Chapter V, paragraphs 31–48 of the Wikisource transcription; opens “It is impossible for language to describe the bitter scowl of rage whi”; closes “edge name and fame that Ivanhoe gives this proud knight the meeting he desires."”.

questions.prompt: Why does Cedric keep commenting on the named knights’ ancestry?
facilitatorNotes: He claims Saxon participation in a victory that others might describe as French or Norman. His satisfaction shows how strongly inherited identity shapes his judgments.
evidence: Of Saxon descent

questions.prompt: What makes the Palmer’s difficulty recalling the sixth knight suspicious to the Templar?
facilitatorNotes: His detailed earlier recollection contrasts with sudden hesitation at a crucial name. Readers may infer strategic restraint while recognizing that hesitation alone cannot prove his motive.
evidence: this assumed forgetfulness

questions.prompt: What different kinds of value do the reliquary and gold chain bring to the challenge?
facilitatorNotes: Sacred meaning and material wealth become public guarantees. Rowena’s offer to answer for Ivanhoe adds personal trust to the formal pledges.
evidence: This reliquary

days.title: The Time Machine — excerpt: A museum after memory
days.challenge: Use material details to follow an identification and then a change of purpose.
days.focus: Preservation, decay and the loss of cultural understanding.
days.context: The Traveller and Weena reach the Palace of Green Porcelain, hoping it may offer shelter and useful objects.
days.contentNote: The Traveller questions Weena’s humanity in a patronizing way; he briefly thinks about weapons. Fossil names and scientific assumptions reflect the edition’s period.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 11; begins "\"I found the Palace of Green Porcelain, when we approached it about"; ends "in possession of powers that might be of use against the Morlocks.".

questions.prompt: How does the Traveller test his first impression that the building is a museum?
facilitatorNotes: Skeletons, display cases and organized galleries accumulate into a supported identification.
evidence: My museum hypothesis was confirmed.

questions.prompt: What contrast appears between fossils intended for preservation and their present uses?
facilitatorNotes: Objects once arranged for knowledge become beads or playthings; survival of an object does not ensure survival of its meaning.
evidence: threaded in strings upon reeds

questions.prompt: Why do machines interest him more than the better-preserved minerals?
facilitatorNotes: His expertise and need for protection shape attention. He seeks practical powers as well as understanding the past.
evidence: I have a certain weakness for mechanism

days.title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — Part I
days.challenge: Track the wedding frame and sea voyage through archaic diction, recurring sounds, and marginal commentary.
days.focus: A compelled act of storytelling and an unexplained violation of hospitality.
days.context: An old sailor stops a guest on his way to a wedding. Read the verse aloud after a first silent pass. The short prose paragraphs between stanzas are the marginal gloss printed beside the poem in this edition, not newly supplied explanation.
days.contentNote: The poem uses Christian and supernatural imagery and ends with the killing of a bird.

excerpt.locator:
The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — Part I; complete verse and marginal gloss of this part. Begins “An ancient Mariner meeteth three Gallants bidden to a wedding-fe”; ends “ds, that plague thee thus!--
  Why look'st thou so?'--With my cross-bow
  I shot the ALBATROSS.”.

questions.prompt: How does the Mariner keep the guest after releasing his hand?
facilitatorNotes: His glittering eye and speech exert a different kind of compulsion; the repeated inability to choose establishes storytelling as a power.
evidence: He cannot choose but hear

questions.prompt: How do sounds change the voyage from celebration into threat?
facilitatorNotes: The cheering departure and wedding music give way to the ice’s cracking, growling, roaring, and howling, making an apparently empty region violently audible.
evidence: It cracked and growled, and roared and howled

questions.prompt: What makes shooting the albatross a violation before any punishment is described?
facilitatorNotes: The bird has been welcomed, fed, and treated as a companion or good omen. The final admission supplies no motive that would explain away the broken hospitality.
evidence: We hailed it in God's name

days.title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — Part II
days.challenge: Compare the sailors’ changing judgments with what the narration and gloss actually establish.
days.focus: Convenient explanations, shared responsibility, and a burden made visible.
days.context: The Mariner has shot the albatross. The ship continues north, but its crew changes its explanation of the bird’s influence.
days.contentNote: The passage depicts extreme thirst, frightening supernatural signs, and a dead bird hung around a man’s neck.

excerpt.locator:
The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — Part II; complete verse and marginal gloss of this part. Begins “The Sun now rose upon the right:
  Out of the sea came he,
  Still hid in m”; ends “oks
  Had I from old and young!
  Instead of the cross, the Albatross
  About my neck was hung.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the sailors first condemn and then approve the same killing?
facilitatorNotes: They change their explanation with the weather: the bird supposedly brought a useful wind, then supposedly brought unwanted mist. Immediate advantage governs their judgment.
evidence: That brought the fog and mist

questions.prompt: How does the painted-ship comparison transform an ordinary calm into imprisonment?
facilitatorNotes: A painting cannot move or change; repeated days and the still image make duration feel trapped rather than restful.
evidence: As idle as a painted ship

questions.prompt: What does the marginal comment about throwing “the whole guilt” on the Mariner add to the final image?
facilitatorNotes: It questions the crew’s effort to shift all blame after they justified the act. The dead bird is a visible burden, while their earlier approval remains part of the moral account.
evidence: throw the whole guilt

days.title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — Part III
days.challenge: Follow the repeated reinterpretation of a distant shape and distinguish survival from rescue.
days.focus: A promised escape turned into a more terrible uncertainty.
days.context: The thirsty crew sees something approaching its motionless ship. The marginal gloss names the supernatural figures more directly than the Mariner’s questions do.
days.contentNote: The sailor bites his arm in desperation; the passage describes the crew’s sudden deaths and uses disease imagery. These are fictional Gothic events, not recommended responses to distress.

excerpt.locator:
The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — Part III; complete verse and marginal gloss of this part. Begins “The ancient Mariner beholdeth a sign in the element afar off.”; ends “They fled to bliss or woe!
  And every soul, it passed me by,
  Like the whizz of my cross-bow!”.

questions.prompt: How does the sequence “a speck, a mist, a shape” make perception into an event?
facilitatorNotes: Each stage revises an uncertain distant impression; readers approach the object with the watcher instead of receiving a stable identification at once.
evidence: A speck, a mist, a shape

questions.prompt: What first makes the approaching ship’s apparent promise of help suspicious?
facilitatorNotes: It advances without breeze or tide; as it crosses the sun, its skeletal structure becomes visible. Details that should signal rescue become signs of impossibility.
evidence: Without a breeze, without a tide

questions.prompt: Why does the final cross-bow sound connect the deaths to the earlier act without explaining every supernatural rule?
facilitatorNotes: The souls’ passage repeats the weapon’s sound, making the killing echo through its consequences. The pattern is symbolically clear even while the exact workings of Death and Life-in-Death remain mysterious.
evidence: Like the whizz of my cross-bow

days.title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — Part IV
days.challenge: Track a change in evaluative language rather than assume the natural creatures themselves transform.
days.focus: Unplanned attention and a movement from disgust toward love.
days.context: The Mariner survives alone among the dead crew. The wedding guest briefly interrupts, afraid that the storyteller may himself be a ghost.
days.contentNote: The poem dwells on dead bodies, isolation, guilt, and inability to pray; its movement toward relief uses a Christian supernatural framework.

excerpt.locator:
The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — Part IV; complete verse and marginal gloss of this part. Begins “The Wedding-Guest feareth that a Spirit is talking to him;”; ends “d pray;
  And from my neck so free
  The Albatross fell off, and sank
  Like lead into the sea.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the wedding guest’s interruption matter after the account of the crew’s deaths?
facilitatorNotes: It reminds readers of the living listener and raises the status of the teller; the Mariner explicitly distinguishes his survival from the others’ deaths.
evidence: This body dropt not down

questions.prompt: What changes between calling sea creatures “slimy things” and watching the water-snakes’ “rich attire”?
facilitatorNotes: The language moves from disgust and comparison with dead humans to detailed color, movement, and beauty; the change occurs in his attention and response.
evidence: Blue, glossy green, and velvet black

questions.prompt: Why does blessing the creatures “unaware” matter to the release that follows?
facilitatorNotes: The blessing is spontaneous rather than a calculated bargain for relief. Prayer and the falling albatross follow a response he did not manufacture as a technique.
evidence: I blessed them unaware

days.title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — Part V
days.challenge: Track several agents of the ship’s movement and a sequence of changing sounds.
days.focus: Relief that does not erase consequence or complete the penance.
days.context: After the Mariner blesses the water-snakes, the albatross falls away and he can pray. Sleep, rain, and renewed motion follow. The edition’s bracketed “inspirited” is a wording variant inside a sidenote.
days.contentNote: Dead sailors’ bodies move under supernatural influence. Christian angelic imagery and continuing punishment shape the episode.

excerpt.locator:
The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — Part V; complete verse and marginal gloss of this part. Begins “Oh sleep! it is a gentle thing,
  Beloved from pole to pole!
  To Mary Quee”; ends “e,
  As soft as honey-dew:
  Quoth he, 'The man hath penance done,
  And penance more will do.'”.

questions.prompt: How does rain answer an earlier bodily need as well as mark an emotional change?
facilitatorNotes: Wet lips, a cold throat, and soaked garments reverse the parching drought; relief is registered through the body, not only announced.
evidence: And still my body drank

questions.prompt: Why does the distinction between returning souls and blessed spirits matter to the wedding guest’s fear?
facilitatorNotes: The Mariner says the dead men’s own souls do not re-enter them. The explanation reframes the eerie movement as angelic assistance, while its appearance remains disturbing.
evidence: But a troop of spirits blest

questions.prompt: How does the final soft voice qualify the apparent progress toward release?
facilitatorNotes: It acknowledges penance already endured but says more remains; the return of motion and beauty is not the end of responsibility.
evidence: And penance more will do

days.title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — Part VI
days.challenge: Separate voices, visible motion, and the Mariner’s uncertain recognition of home.
days.focus: A return that combines welcome with the persistence of fear.
days.context: Two spirits discuss the moving ship. When the Mariner wakes, he is still confronted by the dead crew before the voyage turns homeward.
days.contentNote: The opening uses a historical master-and-slave simile. Dead bodies, fear, and angelic apparitions remain part of the supernatural narrative.

excerpt.locator:
The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — Part VI; complete verse and marginal gloss of this part. Begins “FIRST VOICE”; ends “
  That he makes in the wood.
  He'll shrieve my soul, he'll wash away
  The Albatross's blood.”.

questions.prompt: What does the comparison with a frightened traveler on a lonely road add after the spell breaks?
facilitatorNotes: Release from one constraint does not immediately remove dread; he looks outward yet remains haunted by what may follow him.
evidence: Doth close behind him tread

questions.prompt: How does recognizing the lighthouse, hill, and church connect arrival with the departure in Part I?
facilitatorNotes: The landmarks return in reverse emotional circumstances; familiar objects now provoke astonished questions and a wish that the sight be real.
evidence: Is this mine own countree

questions.prompt: Why can silence sink “like music” after the earlier terrifying silence?
facilitatorNotes: The luminous figures’ signaling and the prospect of help give silence a peaceful significance. The contrast shows that absence of speech takes meaning from its situation.
evidence: Like music on my heart

days.title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — Part VII
days.challenge: Connect the ending’s explanation of storytelling with the opening compulsion and assess the final lesson.
days.focus: Telling as recurrent penance, teaching, and a changed relation to company.
days.context: The pilot, his boy, and a hermit approach the returned ship. The Mariner hopes the hermit can absolve him; “shrieve” means hear confession and grant absolution.
days.contentNote: The ship sinks; the rescue includes fear, distress, and historical language about mental disturbance. The ending expresses a Christian moral vision and remembers an animal killing.

excerpt.locator:
The Rime of the Ancient Mariner — Part VII; complete verse and marginal gloss of this part. Begins “The Hermit of the Wood,”; ends “been stunned,
  And is of sense forlorn:
  A sadder and a wiser man,
  He rose the morrow morn.”.

questions.prompt: How does the requested absolution become a continuing obligation to speak?
facilitatorNotes: The story first relieves his agony, but the pain returns until he tells it again to a particular listener. Rescue does not bring simple silence or final release.
evidence: at an uncertain hour

questions.prompt: Why does walking to church with a company matter beyond the final statement about loving creatures?
facilitatorNotes: He contrasts shared prayer and companionship with the extremity of isolation. The moral is embodied in a newly valued ordinary social action.
evidence: To walk together to the kirk

questions.prompt: Does becoming “a sadder and a wiser man” mean the wedding guest has merely memorized a rule?
facilitatorNotes: His stunned departure and changed next morning suggest an unsettling experience. Readers may debate what wisdom he gains and why it includes sadness rather than only celebration.
evidence: A sadder and a wiser man

days.title: The Time Machine — excerpt: Useful relics and false hopes
days.challenge: Connect comic reversals with the character’s practical and intellectual priorities.
days.focus: What remains useful when institutions have vanished.
days.context: In the ruined museum, the Traveller has taken an iron bar for defense and to force the doors hiding his machine.
days.contentNote: Weapons and failed explosives appear without instructional detail. His treatment of religious objects reflects a dismissive colonial museum viewpoint.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 11; begins "\"Well, mace in one hand and Weena in the other, I went"; ends "to find my bar of iron not altogether inadequate for the work.".

questions.prompt: What does thinking of his own seventeen papers reveal in the ruined library?
facilitatorNotes: The vast loss becomes personal; self-interest and scholarly concern mix instead of producing a purely detached moral.
evidence: my own seventeen papers upon physical optics

questions.prompt: Why does finding matches prompt a dance while surviving guns offer little help?
facilitatorNotes: Matches can still function and the Morlocks fear light; intact-looking weapons lack usable ammunition. Practical usefulness reverses apparent grandeur.
evidence: They were perfectly good.

questions.prompt: How does the failed dynamite test save him from his own plan?
facilitatorNotes: The models cannot explode; real explosives might have destroyed the hidden machine along with the doors. His disappointment is retrospectively fortunate.
evidence: my chances of finding the Time Machine

days.title: The Time Machine — excerpt: Fire in the dark wood
days.challenge: Follow a chain of decisions that seem clever at the time and turn out to be mistakes.
days.focus: Fire, darkness and the Traveller’s responsibility.
days.context: The Traveller and Weena have explored the Palace of Green Porcelain, where he found matches, camphor and an iron bar. As evening falls they set out for the White Sphinx through a dark wood. This passage begins the chapter titled “In the Darkness.”
days.contentNote: The Morlocks attack in darkness; the Traveller fights them with an iron bar, and Weena falls unconscious.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 12; begins ""We emerged from the Palace while the sun was still in part above the "; ends " succulent giving of flesh and bone under my blows, and for a moment I was free.".

questions.prompt: The Traveller lights his gathered wood to “amaze our friends behind.” How does he tell his listeners that this was a mistake before its consequences appear?
facilitatorNotes: His retrospective comment foreshadows disaster and heightens suspense. Students may ask why he did it anyway: sleeplessness, fever and overconfidence all appear in the text.
evidence: I was to discover the atrocious folly of this proceeding

questions.prompt: Why is fire “an altogether new and strange thing” to Weena, and what does this suggest about the Eloi?
facilitatorNotes: The skill of making fire has been forgotten, a sign of decline; her wish to play with the flames shows innocence. Some students may read the explanation as the Traveller’s condescension.
evidence: In this decadence, too, the art of fire-making had been forgotten on the earth.

questions.prompt: How does losing his sense of direction change the Traveller’s plan?
facilitatorNotes: He must stop and build a camp in the wood, which makes sleep and a dying fire the new dangers. This is the turning point of the night.
evidence: now I had not the faintest idea in what direction lay my path
I determined to build a fire and encamp where we were.

questions.prompt: What happens when he falls asleep, and how does his language about the Morlocks change in the fight?
facilitatorNotes: He wakes in darkness with the creatures on him; fear turns into hatred, and he calls them “human rats.” Students may discuss whether his language is justified by his danger.
evidence: I had slept, and my fire had gone out, and the bitterness of death came over my soul.
shaking the human rats from me

days.title: The Time Machine — excerpt: The burning forest
days.challenge: Interpret the Traveller’s changing reactions to the Morlocks once they are helpless.
days.focus: Mercy, horror and grief after the fire.
days.context: Attacked in the dark wood, the Traveller has fought the Morlocks off with his iron bar. Weena lies unconscious somewhere near him. The chapter ends with this passage.
days.contentNote: Morlocks are killed with the bar and in a forest fire, some running blindly into the flames, and the Traveller concludes that Weena has died.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 12; begins ""The strange exultation that so often seems to accompany hard fighting"; ends "cket were still some loose matches. The box must have leaked before it was lost.".

questions.prompt: What does the Traveller realize about the Morlocks’ flight, and what has caused it?
facilitatorNotes: His own careless fire has spread through the forest and saved him, an irony after his “folly.” Students may also note that the same fire may have killed Weena.
evidence: It was my first fire coming after me.
at that I understood the smell of burning wood

questions.prompt: Why does he stop striking the Morlocks on the hillock, and what later tempts him to begin again?
facilitatorNotes: Their helplessness awakens pity; later grief and anger nearly drive him to “a massacre,” but he contains himself. Students can trace the struggle between those impulses.
evidence: I was assured of their absolute helplessness and misery in the glare, and I struck no more of them.
I was almost moved to begin a massacre of the helpless abominations about me, but I contained myself.

questions.prompt: He calls the scene of blind Morlocks “the most weird and horrible thing” he saw in the future. Why might it be more horrible to him than the attack itself?
facilitatorNotes: It shows the suffering and helplessness of humanity’s descendants, and the imagery is almost hellish. Students may disagree about whether pity or disgust dominates.
evidence: the most weird and horrible thing, I think, of all that I beheld in that future age

questions.prompt: How does the Traveller describe his grief for Weena now, compared with how he felt that morning?
facilitatorNotes: Time and the familiar room have softened it to “the sorrow of a dream”; that morning it left him terribly alone. Students may question how fully he valued her, and the passage connects to the frame’s questions about what is real.
evidence: Now, in this old familiar room, it is more like the sorrow of a dream than an actual loss.
But that morning it left me absolutely lonely again—terribly alone.

days.title: Ivanhoe: Honour and Vulnerability
days.challenge: Hold conflicting emotions and motives together instead of assigning each person a single trait.
days.focus: Public honor tested against private attachments and unequal power.
days.context: Ivanhoe’s name has unsettled Cedric. The prior ends the evening; the Templar addresses Isaac as people leave. One short paragraph signed “L. T.” is the author’s own footnote, printed here after the paragraph that cites it.
days.contentNote: This historical novel imagines twelfth-century England through nineteenth-century assumptions. Its national, religious, racial, and class generalizations are perspectives to examine, not reliable descriptions of whole peoples. Historical insults and threats appear in the original text.

excerpt.locator: Ivanhoe (Edinburgh, 1820), Volume I, Chapter V, paragraphs 49–61 of the Wikisource transcription; opens “A crowd of conflicting emotions seemed to have occupied Cedric, and ke”; closes “ated to their retinue and to the other guests their respective places of repose.”. Scott’s “L. T.” footnote is printed after the paragraph that cites it.
excerpt.inlineReason: The library text keeps Scott's footnote reference [1] after "the Exchequer of the Jews" and the note at the end of the chapter, where the transcription places it; this night omits the reference mark and gives the note as a plain paragraph straight after the paragraph that cites it, as its edition statement declares, so it keeps its own text.

blocks.text: A crowd of conflicting emotions seemed to have occupied Cedric, and kept him silent during this discussion. Gratified pride, resentment, embarrassment, chased each other over his broad and open brow, like the shadow of clouds drifting over a harvest-field; while his attendants, on whom the name of the sixth knight seemed to produce an effect almost electrical, hung in suspense upon their master's looks. But when Rowena spoke, the sound of her voice seemed to startle him from his silence.

"Lady," said Cedric, "this beseems not; were further pledge necessary, I myself, offended, and justly offended, as I am, would yet gage my honour for the honour of Ivanhoe. But the wager of battle is complete, even according to the fantastic fashions of Norman chivalry—Is it not, Father Aymer?"
"It is," replied the Prior; "and the blessed relique and rich chain will I bestow safely in the treasury of our convent, until the decision of this warlike challenge."

Having thus spoken, he crossed himself again and again, and after many genuflections and muttered prayers, he delivered the reliquary to Brother Ambrose, his attendant monk, while he himself swept up with less ceremony, but perhaps with no less internal satisfaction, the golden chain, and bestowed it in a pouch lined with perfumed leather, which opened under his arm. "And now, Sir Cedric," he said, "my ears are chiming vespers with the strength of your good wine—permit us another pledge to the welfare of the fair Lady Rowena, and indulge us with liberty to pass to our repose."

"By the rood of Bromholme," said the Saxon, "you do but small credit to your fame, Sir Prior; report speaks you a bonny monk, that would hear the mattin chime ere he quitted his bowl; and, old as I am, I feared to have shame in encountering you. But, by my faith, a Saxon boy of twelve, in my time, would not so soon have relinquished his goblet."

The Prior had his own reasons, however, for persevering in the course of temperance which he had adopted. He was not only a professional peace-maker, but from practice a hater of all feuds and brawls. It was not altogether from a love to his neighbour, or to himself, or from a mixture of both. On the present occasion he had an instinctive apprehension of the fiery temper of the Saxon, and saw the danger that the reckless and presumptuous spirit, of which his companion had already given so many proofs, might at length end by producing some disagreeable explosion. He therefore gently insinuated the incapacity of the native of any other country engaging in the genial conflict of the bowl with the hardy and strong-headed Saxons; something he mentioned, but slightly, about his own holy character, and ended by pressing his proposal to depart to repose.

The grace-cup was accordingly served round, and the guests, after making deep obeisance to their landlord and to the Lady Rowena, arose and mingled in the hall, while the heads of the family, by separate doors, retired with their attendants.
"Unbelieving dog," said the Templar to Isaac the Jew, as he passed him in the throng, "dost thou bend thy course to the tournament?"
"I do so purpose," replied Isaac, bowing in all humility, "if it please your reverend valour."
"Ay," said the Knight, "to gnaw the bowels of our nobles with usury, and to gull women and boys with gauds and toys—I warrant thee store of shekels in thy Jewish scrip."

"Not a shekel, not a silver penny, not a halfling—so help me the God of Abraham!" said the Jew, clasping his hands; "I go but to seek the assistance of some brethren of my tribe to aid me to pay the fine which the Exchequer of the Jews have imposed upon me—Father Jacob be my speed!—I am an impoverished wretch—the very gaberdine I wear is borrowed from Reuben of Tadcaster."
In those days the Jews were subjected to an Exchequer, specially dedicated to that purpose.—L. T.

The Templar smiled sourly as he replied, "Beshrew thee for a false-hearted liar!" and passing onward, as if disdaining farther conference, he communed with his Moslem slaves in a language unknown to the by-standers. The poor Israelite seemed so staggered by the address of the military monk, that the Templar had passed on to the extremity of the hall ere he raised his head from the humble posture which he had assumed, so far as to be sensible of his departure. And when he did look around, it was with the astounded air of one at whose feet a thunderbolt has just burst, and who hears still the astounding report ringing in his ears.

The Abbot and Prior were shortly after marshalled to their sleeping apartments by the steward and the cup-bearer, each attended by two torch-bearers and two servants carrying refreshments, while servants of inferior condition indicated to their retinue and to the other guests their respective places of repose.

questions.prompt: How does the image of sun and cloud describe Cedric more precisely than calling him angry?
facilitatorNotes: Pride in success and resentment toward his son alternate rapidly. The image permits both feelings rather than making one cancel the other.
evidence: conflicting emotions

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator compare the prior’s handling of the relic and the chain?
facilitatorNotes: Different ceremony accompanies similar pleasure in possession. The comparison invites doubt about the separation between his religious and material interests.
evidence: no less internal satisfaction

questions.prompt: How does Isaac’s final response to the Templar differ from the proud challenges exchanged earlier?
facilitatorNotes: His vulnerable position makes deference and silence protective choices. The scene exposes how differently the language of honor works when one person can threaten another.
evidence: the humble posture which he had assumed

days.title: The Time Machine — excerpt: A trap inside a trap
days.challenge: Track repeated reversals in who seems to possess superior knowledge.
days.focus: Overconfidence undone by a small practical omission.
days.context: After the forest fire in which Weena was lost, the Traveller returns alone to the White Sphinx, carrying the machine’s levers. He finds the bronze doors of the pedestal open.
days.contentNote: Physical struggle and a blow to a Morlock’s head are described.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 13; begins "\"And now came a most unexpected thing. As I approached the pedestal"; ends "myself in the same grey light and tumult I have already described.".

questions.prompt: Why does the open entrance seem like surrender and yet suggest a trap?
facilitatorNotes: The machine is accessible after resistance, but its captors can close the doors. The Traveller thinks escape by machine will defeat their plan.
evidence: a meek surrender

questions.prompt: What does the machine’s being cleaned suggest that his contempt for the Morlocks might obscure?
facilitatorNotes: They show mechanical interest and capability; his dismissive language sits beside evidence of purposeful investigation.
evidence: carefully oiled and cleaned

questions.prompt: How does the kind of match transform the scene’s pace and his confidence?
facilitatorNotes: An overlooked need for the box removes light just when he must fit the levers; calm anticipation becomes a tactile scramble.
evidence: light only on the box

days.title: The Time Machine — excerpt: At the edge of life
days.challenge: Attend to changing scale, color and sound in a nearly empty landscape.
days.focus: The limits of human presence and certainty.
days.context: Escaping the Morlocks, the Traveller has gone still farther into the future and reached a shore inhabited by enormous crab-like creatures. He continues toward a dying world.
days.contentNote: A bleak vision of extinction and bodily distress; its astronomical timescale is speculative fiction.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 14; begins "\"I cannot convey the sense of abominable desolation that hung over the"; ends "remote and awful twilight sustained me while I clambered upon the saddle.".

questions.prompt: Why are thousand-year steps described as “great strides” while the changes can still seem small?
facilitatorNotes: Human measures become inadequate beside planetary time; repetition of the red sun and sea makes the eventual loss of life more unsettling.
evidence: great strides of a thousand years or more

questions.prompt: How does listing absent sounds make silence more tangible?
facilitatorNotes: Voices, sheep, birds and insects summon familiar life only to remove it; the remaining sea and wind are called lifeless.
evidence: All the sounds of man

questions.prompt: Why revise the apparent rock into a moving creature near the end?
facilitatorNotes: The uncertain observation prevents a simple declaration that all animal life has ended. A tiny remnant survives his first judgment, without making the world reassuring.
evidence: there was no mistake now that it was a moving thing

days.title: The Time Machine — excerpt: A lie—or a prophecy
days.challenge: Compare the value of a narrative with the question of whether its events are factual.
days.focus: Objects, memory and competing responses to testimony.
days.context: The Traveller has returned to his own time and finished his account to the dinner guests. Weena’s flowers and his damaged machine remain.
days.contentNote: Mild profanity and period language about mental distress appear.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 16; begins "\"I know,\" he said, after a pause, \"that all this will be"; ends "laughed hugely. I remember him standing in the open doorway, bawling good-night.".

questions.prompt: What invitation does he offer by saying to take the account as a prophecy or fiction?
facilitatorNotes: Listeners can examine its implications even if they reject literal time travel. The novel draws attention to its own power as an invented warning.
evidence: Take it as a lie—or a prophecy.

questions.prompt: Why are the flowers suggestive without being decisive proof?
facilitatorNotes: The doctor cannot classify them, but unfamiliarity does not establish their origin; the Traveller’s attachment also prevents an easy specimen exchange.
evidence: I certainly don't know the natural order of these flowers

questions.prompt: How does touching the machine affect the Traveller differently from his listeners?
facilitatorNotes: Its presence restores his memory and confidence; the doctor still attributes the experience to overwork. One object supports different interpretations.
evidence: ran his hand along the damaged rail

days.title: The Time Machine — excerpt: Waiting for the second story
days.challenge: Distinguish unresolved plot from a definite emotional and ethical conclusion.
days.focus: Uncertainty, hope and the meaning of two flowers.
days.context: The unnamed narrator revisits the Traveller the next day, hoping for stronger evidence. This excerpt includes the novel’s epilogue.
days.contentNote: The epilogue uses a demeaning stereotype about prehistoric people and imagines danger; no violent event is narrated.

excerpt.locator: Chapter 16 and Epilogue; begins "I shared a cab with the Editor. He thought the tale a"; ends "and a mutual tenderness still lived on in the heart of man.".

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator remain undecided when the Editor calls the story a “gaudy lie”?
facilitatorNotes: He distinguishes improbable content from credible delivery and chooses further observation rather than immediate belief or rejection.
evidence: the telling so credible and sober

questions.prompt: How does the promise of half an hour change when the narrative reveals three years have passed?
facilitatorNotes: A small social delay expands into permanent uncertainty; promised specimens and photographs remain unavailable.
evidence: The Time Traveller vanished three years ago.

questions.prompt: What can the flowers witness even without proving the whole future history?
facilitatorNotes: They stand for gratitude and mutual tenderness. The ending preserves a value that the narrator can act on despite uncertainty about civilization’s fate.
evidence: gratitude and a mutual tenderness still lived on in the heart of man

days.title: Kubla Khan — the complete published verse fragment
days.challenge: Reread the turn from an imagined landscape to a conditional claim about making poetry.
days.focus: Creative power expressed through music, paradox, and an unfinished wish.
days.context: Coleridge published this poem as a fragment; the whole published verse is supplied here, without the prose preface. Read once for the landscape and again for the change to the speaker’s own imagined performance.
days.contentNote: The poem presents an exoticized imagined Asian court and an “Abyssinian” singer, alongside supernatural and religious imagery. These figures belong to the poem’s imagination, not documentary descriptions of cultures.

excerpt.locator: Kubla Khan, complete published verse fragment, excluding prose preface; begins “In Xanadu did Kubla Khan”; ends “And drunk the milk of Paradise.”

questions.prompt: How do the ordered gardens and the violent fountain produce different kinds of power?
facilitatorNotes: Walls and measured ground express deliberate design, while the chasm and erupting rocks suggest a force beyond such control. Their coexistence makes the pleasure-dome unstable as well as splendid.
evidence: ceaseless turmoil seething

questions.prompt: Why does the combination of a sunny dome and caves of ice deserve the phrase “miracle of rare device”?
facilitatorNotes: It joins opposed sensations and spaces into one imagined construction, whose possibility belongs to poetic vision rather than an ordinary building plan.
evidence: A sunny pleasure-dome with caves of ice

questions.prompt: What remains conditional in the last movement, even while its language becomes commanding?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker first says that if he could revive the singer’s music, he would build the dome in air. The later warnings dramatize that imagined power without confirming that the recovery has occurred.
evidence: Could I revive within me
